stem: A 34-year-old healthy woman presents with recurrent symptoms, including headache, anxiety, and mastalgia, that start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward
why_right: Headache, anxiety and mastalgia that start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward are luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menses, which is the defining pattern of premenstrual (tension) syndrome. She is otherwise healthy and the symptoms are recurrent and cyclic, so this is a clinical diagnosis made from the timing alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometriosis gives dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia and infertility; it does not cause luteal mood and breast symptoms that vanish with the period.
B. Perimenopause gives hot flushes and irregular cycles in an older woman, not symptoms locked to the week before each menses at age 34.
C. Pelvic congestion syndrome causes chronic dull pelvic pain worse on standing (pelvic varices, multiparous women), not cyclic headache, anxiety and breast pain.
key_concept:
Timing relative to menses decides the diagnosis.
  • Symptoms in luteal phase, gone by early menses: PMS (clinical diagnosis, prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles)
  • Pain starting with menses, normal exam, young: primary dysmenorrhea
  • Dysmenorrhea + dyspareunia + infertility: endometriosis
  • Severe mood symptoms with functional impairment: PMDD
  • No lab or imaging test confirms PMS
exam_pearl: Symptoms BEFORE menses that resolve WITH menses = PMS; pain that STARTS with menses = dysmenorrhea.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presented with crampy, lower abdominal pain beginning with the onset of menses every month, and lasting for 2 to 3 days. There was no pain between menses, but reported radiation of pain to the lower back and upper thighs, along with nausea, fatigue, and headache which has been present for several years and progressively getting worse. Physical examination normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: beginning with the onset of menses
why_right: A 19-year-old with crampy pain that begins with the onset of menses and lasts 2 to 3 days, radiating to the back and thighs with nausea, fatigue and headache, and a normal examination, is the textbook picture of primary dysmenorrhea: prostaglandin-mediated pain with no pelvic pathology.
why_wrong_block:
A. Secondary dysmenorrhea is pain from pelvic pathology (endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID); suspect it with onset later in life, pain outside menses, dyspareunia or abnormal findings, none of which are present.
B. Premenstrual syndrome starts in the luteal phase, days before menses, and resolves early in menstruation; here the pain starts with menses and there is no pain beforehand.
D. Endometriosis gives secondary dysmenorrhea, often with dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, infertility or nodularity and a fixed uterus on exam; the exam here is normal and the timing is confined to menses.
key_concept:
Pain timing + exam decides dysmenorrhea type.
  • Primary: young, starts with menses, 1 to 3 days, normal exam → NSAIDs, then COCP
  • Secondary: older onset, pelvic pathology, abnormal exam → ultrasound, treat cause
  • PMS: luteal-phase symptoms that ease once menses begins
  • Worsening pain over years is a reason to reassess for secondary causes, but with a normal exam and classic timing the diagnosis stays primary
exam_pearl: Symptoms before menses = PMS; pain starting with menses + normal exam = primary dysmenorrhea.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1991).

stem: A 30 something or late twenties woman complains of secondary amenorrhea for 6 month , normal FSH and prolactin, what is the diagnosis ? ( question had short stem, no labs mentioned)
why_right: In a woman in her late twenties or thirties with 6 months of secondary amenorrhea, a normal FSH rules out ovarian failure and a normal prolactin rules out hyperprolactinemia. Of the remaining causes, PCOS is the commonest endocrine cause of secondary amenorrhea, and it typically shows normal FSH (often with raised LH and hyperandrogenism).
why_wrong_block:
A. Premature ovarian failure has high FSH and LH with low estrogen; normal FSH excludes it. Right when FSH is in the menopausal range before 40.
B. A nonspecific label that does not name a recognized diagnosis; it does not explain the picture better than PCOS.
C. Central HPO axis failure (hypogonadotropic) is suggested by low FSH and LH with low estrogen, usually with stress, weight loss or exercise clues; with PCOS available, it is the less likely choice.
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: pregnancy test first, then FSH, prolactin and TSH.
  • High FSH: premature ovarian insufficiency
  • High prolactin: prolactinoma, drugs, hypothyroidism
  • High TSH: hypothyroidism
  • Normal FSH and prolactin: PCOS (most common) or hypothalamic causes
  • Normal hormones after D&C: Asherman syndrome
exam_pearl: The same stem without a PCOS option is keyed to HPO axis failure; when PCOS is listed, choose PCOS.

stem: 19 years old female with primary amenorrhea and present breast development and secondary characteristics most probable diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: present breast development and secondary characteristics
why_right: Primary amenorrhea at 19 with normal breast development and secondary sexual characteristics means the ovaries make estrogen normally, so the defect is in the outflow tract. Mullerian agenesis (MRKH) is a 46,XX woman with normal ovaries but an absent uterus and upper vagina, and it is the classic answer for this pattern.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gonadal dysgenesis (e.g. Turner) gives streak gonads, low estrogen and absent breast development with high FSH. Right when breasts are absent, especially with short stature.
B. LH deficiency is a hypogonadotropic state with low estrogen, so normal breast development would not occur.
D. Pituitary FSH deficiency also gives low estrogen and poor secondary sexual development, not the normal breasts described.
key_concept:
Primary amenorrhea: sort by breasts and uterus.
  • No breasts, high FSH: gonadal dysgenesis (Turner)
  • No breasts, low FSH: hypothalamic or pituitary failure (e.g. Kallmann)
  • Breasts present, uterus absent, normal pubic hair, female testosterone: Mullerian agenesis (MRKH)
  • Breasts present, uterus absent, scant pubic hair, male testosterone: androgen insensitivity
  • Breasts present, uterus present, cyclic pain: imperforate hymen or transverse septum
exam_pearl: Breasts present with absent uterus: check pubic hair and testosterone (or karyotype) to separate MRKH from androgen insensitivity.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A second version is shown under the same number: 'Q 19 y.o female with primary amenorrhea, normal physical examination with normal breast development, what is the cause? A. Müllerin syndrome B. Gonadal agenesis C. Pituitary hormone D. Ovarian' Answer: A (Müllerian), same answer concept.

stem: A 39-year-old G6P5 woman at 24 weeks' gestation presents to the antenatal clinic complaining of decreased fetal movement for the last 24 hours. She is hemodynamically stable. An ultrasound is performed and confirms intrauterine fetal death (fetal demise) with no cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management to induce labor?
why_right: No cardiac activity at 24 weeks is intrauterine fetal death (loss at 20 weeks or more). In a stable woman, labor is induced medically, and at this mid-trimester gestation misoprostol is the main inducing agent because it ripens the cervix and causes contractions effectively when the uterus is still relatively insensitive to oxytocin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin works poorly in the second trimester because uterine oxytocin receptors are few; it is used nearer term or to augment labor once established.
C. Mifepristone is an antiprogestogen used to prime the uterus 36 to 48 hours before misoprostol; it shortens the induction interval but is rarely enough to induce labor on its own.
D. Dinoprostone (PGE2) is mainly used for cervical ripening near term; misoprostol is preferred for induction after mid-trimester fetal death.
key_concept:
Fetal death: confirm, counsel, then deliver.
  • Below 20 weeks: abortion terminology (missed abortion)
  • 20 weeks or more: IUFD
  • Stable, intact membranes: vaginal birth by medical induction
  • Regimen: mifepristone priming then misoprostol
  • Investigate the cause after delivery
exam_pearl: Mifepristone is the primer, misoprostol is the inducer; when asked what induces labor, pick misoprostol.

stem: Woman with amenorrhea. mass felt from vagina during DRE. Diagonal incision across the hymen was done. what prophylactic med
highlight_terms_source: mass felt from vagina during DRE
why_wrong_block:
A. OCPs for 6 months suppress menses, as used for endometriosis; they do nothing to keep the hymenal opening patent after incision.
B. Draining a hematocolpos through a hymenotomy is a minor clean procedure; antibiotics are given only if the collection is infected (pyocolpos), and they do nothing for healing or patency of the new opening, which is what the prophylaxis targets.
C. An IUD is contraception and would not be placed into a freshly incised outflow tract; it has no role in preventing restenosis.
key_concept:
Imperforate hymen: primary amenorrhea with normal secondary sex characteristics and cyclic pain.
  • Bulging bluish membrane at the introitus
  • Hematocolpos felt as a mass on rectal exam or seen on ultrasound
  • Treatment: cruciate or elliptical hymenotomy with drainage
  • Aftercare aims to keep the opening patent
exam_pearl: Normal breasts, cyclic pain and a midline pelvic mass with primary amenorrhea point to outflow obstruction, not a hormonal cause.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'Topical Estrogen', which is not among the listed options.

stem: A question about retained placenta for 30 min
why_right: Between the two options, IV oxytocin is the correct uterotonic when the placenta is retained for 30 minutes: it produces rhythmic contractions that can help separation and expulsion and limit bleeding while manual removal is arranged. The key point is choosing the safe uterotonic over ergometrine.
why_wrong_block: B. Ergometrine causes sustained tonic contraction, including of the lower segment and cervix, which can trap the placenta inside the uterus; it is also contraindicated in hypertension.
key_concept:
Retained placenta algorithm.
  • Wait 30 minutes after delivery of the baby with active management
  • Still undelivered: manual removal under anesthesia with antibiotics
  • Failed or incomplete removal: dilatation and curettage
  • Adherent placenta (accreta): consider conservative or surgical options
exam_pearl: If manual removal of the placenta is offered at 30 minutes, it beats any further drug.

stem: Woman pregnant 9 weeks gestation presenting with signs of hyperthyroidism but no eye protrusion what’s treatment
why_right: At 9 weeks she is in the first trimester, when propylthiouracil is the preferred antithyroid drug because methimazole carries a higher risk of embryopathy during organogenesis. The choice of drug is driven by the trimester; no eye protrusion does not change it, and radioiodine and surgery are not first line in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methimazole is preferred from the second trimester onward (switch to avoid PTU liver toxicity), but is avoided in the first trimester due to teratogenic risk.
C. Thyroidectomy in pregnancy is reserved for failure or intolerance of antithyroid drugs or a large compressive goiter, and if needed is done in the second trimester.
D. Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it ablates the fetal thyroid.
key_concept:
Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy.
  • First trimester: PTU
  • Second and third trimesters: switch to methimazole
  • Beta blocker: short term symptom control
  • Surgery: second trimester, only if medical therapy fails
  • Radioiodine: never in pregnancy
  • Transient hCG related thyrotoxicosis (often with hyperemesis, no goiter or eye signs): usually supportive care, no antithyroid drug
exam_pearl: Check the gestational age first: before about 12 to 13 weeks choose PTU, after that methimazole.

stem: A 30-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 presented 3 days ago to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with preterm premature rupture of membranes. She was managed expectantly and today she started to have fever and abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: PPROM managed expectantly for 3 days is a major risk factor for ascending intrauterine infection. New fever and abdominal pain after prolonged ROM is chorioamnionitis until proven otherwise; other supportive signs are uterine tenderness, foul discharge, and maternal or fetal tachycardia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Labor causes painful contractions but not fever; fever after prolonged ROM points to infection (which may itself trigger labor).
C. Abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding and a tense, tender uterus, not fever; choose it when bleeding with pain is the lead clue.
D. Cervical incompetence causes painless second-trimester cervical dilation, not fever and pain after ROM.
key_concept:
Fever after PPROM = chorioamnionitis.
  • Clues: fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge, maternal/fetal tachycardia
  • Treatment: IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin) and delivery
  • Tocolysis contraindicated
  • Painful bleeding + tense uterus = abruption instead
exam_pearl: Fever is the word that turns PPROM into chorioamnionitis; without fever or bleeding, think labor.

stem: A 30-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 presented 3 days ago to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with preterm premature rupture of membranes. She was managed conservatively, and today she started to have fever and abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Ampicillin, Gentamicin, and deliver the patient
OptD: Check the source of fever and treat accordingly
why_right: PPROM at 30 weeks managed conservatively for "3 days" now with "fever and abdominal pain" is clinical chorioamnionitis until proven otherwise; prolonged rupture of membranes is its main risk factor. Intra-amniotic infection ends expectant management: give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ampicillin plus gentamicin) and deliver, regardless of gestational age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Analgesia alone ignores an intrauterine infection that threatens mother and fetus and needs antibiotics plus delivery.
B. Antibiotics without delivery are inadequate; continuing pregnancy with chorioamnionitis increases maternal sepsis and neonatal infection. Observation fits uncomplicated PPROM only.
D. In PPROM, fever with abdominal pain is presumed chorioamnionitis; searching for another source delays the required treatment.
key_concept:
PPROM: expectant management until a reason to deliver appears.
  • Uncomplicated: latency antibiotics (ampicillin + erythromycin), steroids <34 weeks, MgSO4 <32 weeks
  • Deliver if: chorioamnionitis, abruption, non-reassuring CTG, high risk of cord prolapse
  • Chorioamnionitis signs: fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge, maternal/fetal tachycardia
  • Chorioamnionitis: IV ampicillin + gentamicin and delivery; tocolysis contraindicated
exam_pearl: Antibiotics alone is the trap: chorioamnionitis always means antibiotics AND delivery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Follow-up 'Q:' variant under 2284 (on p579).

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents at 29 weeks of gestation with prelabor premature rupture of membranes for 7 days. Examination revealed she is having lower abdominal pain, rigors, and fever with purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: prelabor premature rupture of membranes for 7 days
why_right: Membranes ruptured 7 days ago (prolonged PPROM) give an ascending route for infection. Now fever, rigors, lower abdominal pain and purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge are the clinical picture of chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection).
why_wrong_block:
B. Urinary tract infection: causes dysuria, frequency or loin pain with fever; it does not produce purulent foul vaginal discharge after ruptured membranes.
C. Antepartum hemorrhage: presents with vaginal bleeding (painless in previa, painful in abruption), not fever with purulent discharge.
D. Lower respiratory tract infection: would give cough, dyspnea and chest signs, not abdominal pain with foul vaginal discharge.
key_concept:
Prolonged ROM + fever + uterine tenderness/abdominal pain + foul discharge = chorioamnionitis.
  • May also show maternal and fetal tachycardia
  • Treatment: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ampicillin + gentamicin) AND delivery
  • Tocolysis is contraindicated
  • Chorioamnionitis is an indication to end expectant PPROM management
exam_pearl: In PPROM, fever is chorioamnionitis until proven otherwise; the next step is antibiotics plus delivery, not tocolysis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2488).
Compiler note: Variant under 2284 (on p579): compiler's typed 'Q:' version (PPROM 7 days, answer Chorioamnionitis) plus screenshot 0502 of the same question, Answer: A.

stem: Primigravida mother I think was around 20-25 years of age she no medical history or family history of DM. Bp was 110/70. HR was normal (can't remember exact number). What you want to do for her or what you recommend.
highlight_terms_source: no medical history or family history of DM
why_right: This is a low-risk primigravida: young, normotensive, with no personal or family history of DM. For such a woman the routine antenatal recommendation that applies to every pregnancy is iron (with folic acid) supplementation, because pregnancy raises iron demand and iron deficiency anemia is the commonest anemia of pregnancy. Nothing in the stem justifies stepping outside routine care.
why_wrong_block: A. Early glucose screening is reserved for high-risk women (e.g. previous GDM, obesity, strong family history, previous macrosomia); she has none, so she is screened routinely at 24-28 weeks instead.
key_concept:
Low-risk pregnancy = routine care; extra tests only for stated risk factors.
  • Iron + folic acid: routine for all pregnant women
  • GDM screening, average risk: 24-28 weeks
  • Early GDM screening: previous GDM or other high-risk features
  • Microcytic anemia not responding to iron: think thalassemia trait
exam_pearl: Early glucose screening becomes the answer only when the stem gives a risk factor such as previous GDM; "no DM history" is the clue against it.

stem: Female 38 wkf of gestation with twins in vertex position ctg was normal what type of deliver
why_right: Twins at 38 weeks (term) with both in vertex presentation and a normal CTG have no indication for operative delivery. Mode of delivery in twins is decided by the presentation of the first (presenting) twin; vertex-vertex twins are delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Forceps is an operative vaginal delivery that needs a specific second-stage indication (prolonged second stage, fetal compromise) with full dilatation and an engaged head at or below the ischial spines; none is given.
C. Cesarean section is for a non-cephalic first twin, monoamniotic twins or other obstetric indications (fetal distress, obstructed labor); not for vertex-vertex twins with a normal CTG.
key_concept:
Twin delivery is decided by twin A's presentation.
  • Vertex / vertex: vaginal delivery
  • Vertex / non-vertex: vaginal delivery acceptable
  • Twin A non-vertex (breech or transverse): cesarean section
  • Instrumental delivery: only with full dilatation, engaged head at or below the spines, plus an indication
exam_pearl: If twin A is breech the answer flips to cesarean section; twin B's lie alone does not mandate it.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks gestation with a breech presentation is planned for a Cesarean section. During surgery, you notice a right ovarian cyst measuring 12 cm. What will you do?
why_right: An ovarian cyst found during surgery for another cause (here a cesarean for breech) is removed, and in a 22-year-old the ovary-sparing operation is cystectomy. The 12 cm size is a second indication on its own (larger than 5 cm), and removal gives tissue for histology and prevents later torsion or rupture.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oophorectomy sacrifices the whole ovary in a young woman; it is reserved for when the ovary cannot be preserved or malignancy is strongly suspected in an older patient.
C. No intervention fits only a simple, asymptomatic cyst of 5 cm or less found on imaging; a 12 cm cyst seen with the abdomen already open should be removed.
D. Squeezing or rupturing the cyst spills its contents (possibly malignant cells or dermoid material), gives no histology and leaves the cyst wall to recur.
key_concept:
Adnexal mass rule:
  • Simple, asymptomatic, 5 cm or less: observe, repeat US in 6-8 weeks
  • Complex, symptomatic, larger than 5 cm, or found at other surgery: cystectomy
  • Complex mass in a postmenopausal woman: gynecologic oncology
  • Young woman: ovary-sparing cystectomy over oophorectomy
exam_pearl: "Found during cesarean" alone triggers cystectomy, whatever the size.

stem: A 30-year-old Primigravida at 17 weeks of gestation is known to have epilepsy and is on valproic acid, She was concerned about the possible risks to her baby. Which of the following fetal abnormalities is markedly increased?
why_right: Valproic acid is the most teratogenic of the common antiepileptics, and its signature effect is a markedly increased risk of neural tube defects (especially spina bifida), arising from exposure during neural tube closure in the first weeks of pregnancy (interference with folate metabolism is one proposed mechanism). At 17 weeks the concern is screened for with the anomaly scan and maternal serum AFP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oligohydramnios reflects fetal renal agenesis or obstruction, uteroplacental insufficiency or ruptured membranes, not valproate exposure.
B. Polyhydramnios is linked to maternal diabetes, multiple gestation and impaired fetal swallowing (e.g. anencephaly, duodenal atresia); it is not the direct valproate effect.
D. Non-immune hydrops follows fetal cardiac disease, parvovirus infection, chromosomal anomalies or severe fetal anemia, not valproate.
key_concept:
Antiepileptic teratogenicity: match the drug to its defect.
  • Valproate: neural tube defects (spina bifida), highest overall malformation risk
  • Carbamazepine: neural tube defects (lower risk), craniofacial defects
  • Phenytoin: fetal hydantoin syndrome (craniofacial, nail and digit hypoplasia)
  • Lamotrigine, levetiracetam: preferred in pregnancy
  • On antiepileptics: high-dose folic acid before conception
exam_pearl: Valproate = neural tube defect; the amniotic fluid options are distractors.

stem: Pregnant women at 10 wks of gestation with previous 2 abortion due to congenital anomalies come. When is the time for screening for anomalies:
highlight_terms_source: previous 2 abortion due to congenital anomalies
why_right: She is booking at 10 weeks with a history of losses from congenital anomalies, so she needs a detailed anomaly (morphology) scan. That scan is done at 18-22 weeks, when fetal organs are large enough for a complete anatomical survey yet early enough to allow counselling and decisions; 18-20 weeks is the option within that window.
why_wrong_block:
A. 10-12 weeks is the dating scan window (confirm gestational age, viability, number of fetuses), too early for detailed anatomy.
B. 12-14 weeks covers first-trimester aneuploidy screening (nuchal translucency), not the detailed structural survey; organs are still too small.
D. 22-26 weeks is later than the standard window; anomalies found then leave fewer management options.
key_concept:
Antenatal scan timing:
  • Dating scan: 10-11 weeks
  • Nuchal translucency (aneuploidy screen): late first trimester
  • Anomaly (morphology) scan: 18-22 weeks
  • Previous anomaly does not move the anomaly scan earlier
exam_pearl: A high-risk history changes how carefully the anomaly scan is done, not its timing: still 18-22 weeks.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No answer on typed version; embedded screenshot 0499 (same question: 25-year-old at 10 weeks, previous IUFD with multiple congenital anomalies, best time for detailed anomaly scan; options 10-12, 14-16, 18-22, 24-28 weeks) gives Answer: C (18-22 weeks).

stem: A 22-year-old PG at 39 weeks of gestation admitted to the Labor Room with active labor. Initial cervical examination revealed 5 cm dilatation with 60% effacement and station was at -2. After 6 hours despite regular adequate contractions, abdominal examination revealed the presence of a retraction ring and vaginal examination showed cervical dilatation of 7 cm and station of -1. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: She is a term primigravida in active labor who advanced only from 5 cm to 7 cm and from -2 to -1 "after 6 hours despite regular adequate contractions". The decisive clue is a retraction ring (Bandl ring) on abdominal examination, which is pathognomonic of obstructed labor and signals impending uterine rupture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Preterm labor is labor before 37 weeks; she is at 39 weeks (term).
C. Chorioamnionitis would show fever, maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness or foul liquor; none are described.
D. Abruptio placentae presents with painful vaginal bleeding, a tense tender uterus and fetal distress, not a retraction ring with arrested progress.
key_concept:
Bandl (pathological retraction) ring = obstructed labor until proven otherwise.
  • Forms between a thick upper active segment and a thinned overstretched lower segment
  • Rises toward the umbilicus, visible or palpable abdominally
  • Risk: uterine rupture
  • Management: urgent cesarean section, never oxytocin
exam_pearl: Slow progress alone suggests arrest; add a palpable retraction ring and it becomes obstructed labor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0234.

stem: Pregnant known diabetic 40weeks uneventful pregnancy, sudden fetal death, fetus was 2.6kg no obvious anomaly, placental sample showed thrombi, what's the cause of the fetal death:
why_right: The decisive clue is the pathology: the placental sample showed thrombi, with no anomaly and an otherwise uneventful pregnancy. Placental thrombosis and infarction cut off uteroplacental blood flow and are a direct, demonstrated cause of sudden fetal death, so the death is attributed to the placental abnormality. Diabetes is a background risk factor, but the question asks for the cause shown by the findings.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pregestational diabetes raises the risk of stillbirth, but it is the predisposing condition; the proven mechanism here is the placental thrombosis found on histology.
C. A 2.6 kg baby at 40 weeks is small but not proof of growth restriction as the cause; any reduced growth would itself result from the placental disease, and the stem says the pregnancy was uneventful.
key_concept:
Cause of death = the lesion demonstrated, not the background risk factor.
  • Pregestational DM: macrosomia or IUGR, polyhydramnios, pre-eclampsia, single umbilical artery, stillbirth
  • Placental thrombi or infarcts: reduced perfusion, IUGR, oligohydramnios, IUFD
  • IUFD: loss at 20 weeks or more
exam_pearl: When the stem hands you a placental finding, the answer is the placenta; diabetes is the distractor that "caused the cause".

stem: 34 year old G2P1 pregnant found out that her baby has Single umbilical artery, she has hx of a multiple pregnancy, and hypothyroidism on thyroxine. what is the risk factors?
why_right: Single umbilical artery is clearly more frequent in multiple pregnancies, the strongest recognised risk factor among the options. The other classic association, maternal (pregestational) diabetes, is not offered; her age of 34, low parity (G2P1) and treated hypothyroidism are weak or unrecognised associations.
why_wrong_block:
A. Only advanced maternal age (around 40 and above) shows a weak link to single umbilical artery; at 34 she is below that, and age matters mainly for aneuploidy risk.
B. Parity has at most a weak, inconsistent association with single umbilical artery, and G2P1 is low parity; parity matters more for PPH from atony in grand multiparas.
D. Treated hypothyroidism on thyroxine is not a recognised association; maternal diabetes is the endocrine risk factor to remember.
key_concept:
Single umbilical artery: associations to know.
  • Multiple pregnancy
  • Maternal diabetes (pregestational)
  • Fetal chromosomal and structural anomalies (renal, cardiac)
  • Isolated finding: arrange detailed anomaly scan and growth monitoring
exam_pearl: If "diabetes" were an option it would compete strongly; here multiple pregnancy is the only listed true association.

stem: 23 weeks primagravida came with minimal vaginal spotting, no pain, no contractions. US showed viable baby with cervical length of 30mm, most appropriate management?
OptD: induction? C sec? I can’t remember
why_right: A primigravida has no previous second trimester loss, so she follows the cervical length pathway, and her cervix is 30 mm, above the 25 mm threshold. With only minimal spotting, no pain, no contractions and a viable fetus, there is no sign of preterm labor or cervical insufficiency, so management is conservative (routine antenatal care with observation and reassurance).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cerclage needs a previous second trimester loss (history-indicated) or a cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks in a woman with that history; she has neither.
C. Antenatal corticosteroids are given when preterm delivery is expected imminently (preterm labor, PPROM, bleeding requiring delivery); a long closed cervix with no contractions does not justify them.
D. Induction or cesarean section has no place at 23 weeks with a stable mother and a viable fetus showing no compromise; delivery would only cause extreme prematurity.
key_concept:
Cervical length pathway (no previous mid-trimester loss):
  • Cervix more than 25 mm: routine care
  • Cervix less than 25 mm: vaginal progesterone
  • Previous mid-trimester loss: history-indicated cerclage at 13-14 weeks
  • Previous loss with cervix less than 25 mm at 16-24 weeks: cerclage
  • Cerclage generally not after 24 weeks
exam_pearl: Same stem with cervix 20 mm: still no cerclage in a primigravida; give vaginal progesterone.

stem: A 26-Year-Old Woman Of Average Size Has Delivered A Baby Boy Within The Last 24 Hours. Her Blood Group Is B-Negative, Her Husband Is O-Positive, And Her Newborn Son Is A-Positive. A 300 μg Dose Of Anti-D Immunoglobulin Has Been Prescribed. Which Of The Following Volume Of Fetal Blood Will Be Protected By The Prescribed Dose?
why_right: An Rh negative mother who has just delivered an Rh positive baby needs anti-D within 72 hours to prevent sensitization. The standard dose of 300 micrograms (printed as "300-g") neutralizes about 30 mL of fetal whole blood, which equals about 15 mL of fetal red cells. The ABO groups in the stem are distractors.
why_wrong_block:
A. 15 mL is the red cell equivalent of the dose; as whole blood it covers 30 mL.
C. 60 mL of whole blood would need two standard doses; a bleed that large is found by a Kleihauer test and dosed accordingly.
D. This confuses whole blood with red cells: 300 micrograms covers about 15 mL of D positive red cells, not 30 mL.
key_concept:
Standard postpartum anti-D dose and its coverage.
  • 300 micrograms = 30 mL fetal whole blood = about 15 mL fetal red cells
  • Give within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh positive baby
  • Also given routinely at 28 weeks; the 28-week dose does not replace the postpartum dose
  • Larger bleed suspected: quantify with a Kleihauer test and give extra doses
exam_pearl: Whole blood vs red cells is the trap: the same dose covers 30 mL of whole blood but only 15 mL of red cells.

stem: 32 yo woman w choriocarcinoma + lung mets. Stage III + WHO prognostic score of 10. Rx?
key_concept:
GTN treatment = chemotherapy, intensity chosen by the WHO score.
  • Score 6 or less: low risk, single-agent (methotrexate or actinomycin D)
  • Score 7 or more: high risk, multi-agent (EMA-CO)
  • Lung metastases = stage III; chest X-ray for staging
  • Choriocarcinoma: clinical diagnosis, biopsy avoided (vascular)
  • Hysterectomy: adjunct only, not primary for metastatic disease
exam_pearl: Stage alone does not choose treatment; apply the WHO score: 6 or less single agent, 7 or more multi-agent.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 37-year-old G3 P1011 at 28 weeks' gestation had vaginal spotting 2 weeks ago but no abdominal cramping or passing any clots or tissue. Examination reveals fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks' size. Ultrasound confirms lack of fetal heart activity and no fetal movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: At "28 weeks' gestation" with "lack of fetal heart activity and no fetal movement", the loss is beyond the 20 week cutoff, so the term is fetal demise (intrauterine fetal death), not abortion. The "fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks" fits a fetus that died some weeks earlier, consistent with the spotting 2 weeks ago.
why_wrong_block:
B. Missed abortion is a nonviable pregnancy retained with a closed os, but it is defined BEFORE 20 weeks; at 28 weeks the correct term is fetal demise.
C. Incomplete abortion is also a before 20 weeks term and needs an open os with partial passage of tissue; no tissue or clots were passed here.
D. Gestational trophoblastic disease gives a uterus LARGER than dates, very high hCG and a snowstorm pattern; here the uterus is small and a fetus is seen.
key_concept:
Name the loss by gestational age first.
  • Before 20 weeks: abortion (classify by os and tissue)
  • 20 weeks or more (or weight above 350 g): fetal demise / IUFD
  • Missed abortion: closed os, nonviable, nothing expelled
  • Incomplete: open os, partial tissue passage
  • Uterus large for dates + no fetus: think molar pregnancy
exam_pearl: Same picture as a missed abortion but past 20 weeks = fetal demise.

stem: 47-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities, including obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), presents with heavy menstrual bleeding secondary to uterine fibroids. She has completed her family and prefers a non-surgical treatment. What is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Counsel her that the definitive treatment is hysterectomy
why_right: She has symptomatic fibroids (heavy menstrual bleeding), has completed her family, prefers non-surgical treatment and carries anesthetic risk from multiple comorbidities including OSA. Uterine artery embolization is the effective, durable option for a symptomatic woman who declines or is unfit for surgery, and it is done under sedation without general anesthesia.
why_wrong_block:
A. GnRH agonists shrink fibroids only temporarily, cause menopausal symptoms and bone loss, and are used short-term before surgery; not a definitive non-surgical treatment.
C. Hysterectomy is the definitive cure for a woman with a completed family who accepts surgery, but she has declined surgery and is a higher anesthetic risk, so this ignores her preference.
D. Myomectomy is a surgical, fertility-sparing option for women wanting future pregnancy; she wants neither surgery nor fertility.
key_concept:
Fibroid ladder:
  • Asymptomatic incidental: observe, yearly US
  • Medical: OCP or other hormonal control; GnRH agonist pre-operatively to shrink
  • Refuses or unfit for surgery: uterine artery embolization
  • Surgery for large fibroid (over 7 cm) or failed medical therapy
  • Wants fertility: myomectomy; family complete: hysterectomy
exam_pearl: Wants fertility: myomectomy. Family complete and accepts surgery: hysterectomy. Declines surgery: UAE.

stem: Female at 39w of gestation, Examination shows polyhydramnios, Which Condition might be associated with her?
why_right: Polyhydramnios results from too little fetal swallowing or too much fetal urine. Trisomy 21 is associated with duodenal atresia (and esophageal or swallowing problems), which prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, so fluid accumulates. Among the options it is the only condition linked to excess, rather than reduced, fluid.
why_wrong_block:
B. Renal agenesis means no fetal urine production, causing severe oligohydramnios (Potter sequence), the opposite finding.
C. IUGR from uteroplacental insufficiency reduces fetal renal perfusion and urine output, giving oligohydramnios.
D. Pneumothorax is not a fetal cause of abnormal amniotic fluid; the lung problem linked to fluid volume is pulmonary hypoplasia, a consequence of oligohydramnios.
key_concept:
Amniotic fluid = fetal urine in, fetal swallowing out.
  • Polyhydramnios: maternal DM, multiple gestation, isoimmunization, duodenal or esophageal atresia (trisomy 21), anencephaly, TTTS recipient
  • Oligohydramnios: renal agenesis, urinary obstruction, placental insufficiency or IUGR, ROM, TTTS donor
  • Commonest identifiable cause of polyhydramnios: maternal diabetes
exam_pearl: "Can't swallow" or "too much urine" means polyhydramnios; "no kidneys" or "poor placenta" means oligohydramnios.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy had an ultrasound confirming Dichorionic Diamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
why_right: Dichorionic diamniotic twins from a single zygote arise when cleavage happens within the first 0-72 hours (days 0-3), before the chorion has differentiated. Each embryo therefore develops its own chorion and its own amnion. (Dizygotic twins are also always DCDA, but the stem asks about the ovulation to cleavage interval, which is the monozygotic timing.)
why_wrong_block:
B. Cleavage at 4-8 days happens after the chorion has formed but before the amnion, giving monochorionic diamniotic twins, not DCDA.
C. Cleavage at 9-12 days happens after both chorion and amnion have formed, giving monochorionic monoamniotic twins.
D. Cleavage after about day 12-13 is incomplete and produces conjoined twins.
key_concept:
The later the split, the more the twins share.
  • 0-3 days (0-72 h): DCDA
  • 4-8 days: MCDA
  • 9-12 days: MCMA
  • >12-13 days: conjoined
  • Dizygotic twins: always DCDA, same or different sex
exam_pearl: Each later window removes one separate layer: first the chorion goes (MCDA), then the amnion (MCMA), then the bodies themselves (conjoined).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'A (GB)'.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy had an ultrasound confirming Monochorionic Diamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
why_right: Monochorionic diamniotic twins result from monozygotic cleavage at 4-8 days. By then the chorion has already formed, so it is shared, but the amnion has not yet formed, so each twin gets its own amniotic sac.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cleavage at 0-72 hours precedes chorion formation and gives dichorionic diamniotic twins.
C. Cleavage at 9-12 days occurs after the amnion forms, so the twins share one amnion: monochorionic monoamniotic.
D. Cleavage after about day 12-13 is incomplete and produces conjoined twins.
key_concept:
Monozygotic cleavage timing sets chorionicity.
  • 0-3 days: DCDA
  • 4-8 days: MCDA (most common monozygotic type)
  • 9-12 days: MCMA
  • >12-13 days: conjoined
exam_pearl: MCDA means one shared chorion with two amnions, so cleavage happened after the chorion formed (day 4) but before the amnion (day 8).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'B (GB)'.

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy had an ultrasound confirming Monochorionic Monoamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
why_right: In monozygotic twins the membranes depend on when the embryo splits. By days 9 to 12 the chorion and the amnion have both already formed, so the twins share one chorion and one amniotic sac: monochorionic monoamniotic.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0-72 hours: split before the chorion forms, so each twin gets its own chorion and amnion (dichorionic diamniotic).
B. 4-8 days: chorion already formed but not the amnion, giving monochorionic diamniotic twins (the most common monozygotic type).
D. >12 days: the embryonic disc has begun to form, so splitting this late is incomplete and produces conjoined twins.
key_concept:
Monozygotic cleavage timing:
  • 0-3 days (0-72 hours): Di Di
  • 4-8 days: Mono Di
  • 9-12 days: Mono Mono
  • 13 days or later: conjoined
  • Dizygotic twins are always Di Di
exam_pearl: The later the split, the more is shared: chorion first, then amnion, then the body itself.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1725).
Compiler note: Answer given as 'C (GB)'.

stem: An obese young lady presented with irregular periods. Her BMI is 35. What is the most appropriate advice?
OptA: Reassure her that irregular periods are normal
why_right: An obese young woman (BMI 35) with irregular periods most likely has anovulatory cycles driven by obesity and insulin resistance, typically PCOS. Weight reduction and lifestyle modification is first line for every such patient: even modest weight loss can restore ovulation and regular cycles and lowers metabolic risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. Persistent irregular cycles in an obese woman are not normal; chronic anovulation exposes the endometrium to unopposed estrogen and signals metabolic risk, so reassurance alone is inadequate. Reassurance fits irregular cycles in the first couple of years after menarche.
C. The combined OCP regulates cycles in PCOS when pregnancy is not desired, but it is added after or alongside lifestyle change, not instead of it, and at BMI ≥35 its venous thromboembolism risk makes it a less favoured choice.
key_concept:
PCOS / obesity-related oligomenorrhea ladder:
  • Step 1, everyone: weight loss + lifestyle
  • Irregular cycles, no pregnancy wish: combined OCP
  • Wants pregnancy: ovulation induction
  • Insulin resistance: metformin
exam_pearl: "Most appropriate advice" for an obese patient with menstrual or ovulatory problems is weight loss first; drugs come after.

stem: Female diagnosed with pCO and she is trying to conceive what to give :
why_right: PCOS infertility is due to anovulation, so a woman trying to conceive needs ovulation induction, and among the options that is clomiphene citrate, an anti-estrogen that raises FSH release and triggers follicular development. Weight loss should accompany it in overweight patients.
why_wrong_block:
A. The OCP suppresses ovulation and is a contraceptive; it is the choice for cycle regulation and hirsutism when pregnancy is NOT desired.
B. Metformin targets insulin resistance and can be an adjunct (for example with clomiphene resistance), but it is a weak ovulation inducer on its own and is not the main fertility drug.
key_concept:
PCOS treatment depends on the patient's goal:
  • All: lifestyle and weight loss
  • Regular cycles, no pregnancy wish: combined OCP
  • Wants pregnancy: ovulation induction (clomiphene; letrozole in newer guidelines)
  • Clomiphene failure: gonadotropins or ovarian drilling, then IVF
  • Insulin resistance: metformin
exam_pearl: If letrozole is offered as an option, current international PCOS guidance prefers it over clomiphene as first-line ovulation induction.

stem: 39 wks pregnant with IUFD what to do:
OptC: induction of labour with oxytocin and PGE2
why_right: With a confirmed IUFD at 39 weeks the aim is a safe vaginal delivery, so labour is induced: prostaglandins (PGE2, or misoprostol) ripen the cervix and oxytocin is used to induce or augment contractions. Induction avoids the infection and DIC risk of a prolonged retained dead fetus and spares the mother an unnecessary operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cesarean section adds maternal surgical morbidity with no fetal benefit; it is kept for maternal indications (for example transverse lie, placenta previa, prior classical scar, failed induction or maternal instability).
B. Expectant management can be offered only to a stable woman with intact membranes who prefers it, and she may go home briefly to decide; but waiting for spontaneous labour risks infection and coagulopathy over time, so active induction is the standard answer.
key_concept:
IUFD management:
  • Confirm on ultrasound (no cardiac activity)
  • Check maternal stability, CBC, coagulation (DIC risk rises with prolonged retention)
  • Default: induction for vaginal delivery (prostaglandin then oxytocin)
  • Urgent delivery if sepsis, preeclampsia, abruption, DIC or ruptured membranes
  • C/S only for maternal or obstetric indications
exam_pearl: A stable mother with IUFD does not need emergency admission and may take time to decide, but when asked "what to do" the delivery plan is induction, not C/S.

stem: Second trimester pregnant didn't have measles before when to immunize her:
why_right: Measles vaccine (MMR) is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy because of the theoretical risk to the fetus. A non-immune pregnant woman is therefore vaccinated postpartum, before discharge; breastfeeding is not a contraindication.
why_wrong_block: A. Giving a live vaccine "now" in the second trimester is contraindicated. Vaccination now would be right only for inactivated vaccines such as influenza or Tdap, which are given in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Vaccines and pregnancy:
  • Live (MMR, varicella, yellow fever as a rule): avoid in pregnancy, give postpartum
  • Advise avoiding pregnancy for about 1 month after MMR
  • Inactivated (influenza, Tdap): safe and recommended in pregnancy
  • Accidental MMR in pregnancy is not an indication for termination
  • Postpartum MMR is compatible with breastfeeding
exam_pearl: Any live vaccine question in pregnancy flips to "postpartum"; the inactivated ones (flu, Tdap) are the ones given "now".

stem: A 24 year old female G2P1, found to have a 7 week gestation ectopic pregnancy. One dose of methotrexate was given, and the following β-HCG values were measured from dose date: Day 1: 1800 mmol; Day 2: 1200 mmol; Day 3: 400 mmol; Day 4: 70 mmol; Day 5: 70 mmol. Which of the following approach would you do?
OptA: Continue monitoring β-HCG and send home
why_right: After single-dose methotrexate the β-hCG has fallen from 1800 to 70, a drop of more than 95%, which is far beyond the required >15% fall and shows a good response. The short 70 to 70 plateau at a low level is not a failure signal; the correct plan is to send her home and continue serial β-hCG until it is undetectable, with safety advice about pain or bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
B. Immediate surgery is for rupture, hemodynamic instability or a RISING β-hCG after methotrexate; here the level has fallen dramatically.
C. Laparotomy is reserved for an unstable patient with a ruptured ectopic (and laparoscopy is preferred otherwise); she has no instability and her hCG is falling.
D. A further methotrexate dose is for a plateau or fall of <15% between day 4 and day 7; the overall fall here is massive, so more drug is not indicated.
key_concept:
Methotrexate follow-up (compare day 4 vs day 7 β-hCG):
  • Fall >15%: weekly β-hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second dose of methotrexate
  • Rising: surgical management
  • Instability or rupture at any time: surgery
  • A rise from day 1 to day 4 is expected and not failure
exam_pearl: Judge the trend, not one pair of values: a large overall fall with a brief low-level plateau is still a responding ectopic.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presented to the clinic for preconception counseling. She is known to have hypertension and is on ACE inhibitors. Which of the following is the most appropriate for her antihypertensive medication when she gets pregnant?
OptA: Continue on ACE inhibitors as it is safe
OptB: Continue because the benefit outweighs the risk
OptC: Cannot be stopped, so she should not get pregnant
OptD: Switch to alternative antihypertensive due to fetal kidney teratogenicity
why_right: She is a hypertensive woman on an ACE inhibitor planning pregnancy. ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are fetotoxic, mainly affecting fetal kidney development and function (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios), so they should be switched to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive such as labetalol, methyldopa or nifedipine. Preconception counseling is the ideal time to review and change medications.
why_wrong_block:
A. ACE inhibitors are not safe in pregnancy; they are contraindicated because of fetal renal toxicity.
B. The fetal risk is not justified when equally effective, safe alternatives exist; continuing would only be considered if no alternative could control her BP.
C. Pregnancy is not prohibited; the ACE inhibitor can simply be replaced with a safe agent, and her hypertension still needs treatment.
key_concept:
Chronic hypertension planning pregnancy: review medications first and replace teratogenic agents.
  • Stop: ACE inhibitors, ARBs (fetal renal toxicity, oligohydramnios)
  • Use: labetalol (first line), methyldopa, nifedipine
  • Same principle at booking for any chronic disease: medication review comes first
  • Contrast: a well-controlled drug that is not contraindicated (hydroxychloroquine in SLE) is continued
exam_pearl: Pregnancy plus ACEi/ARB = switch, never continue; continue only drugs that are safe or not absolutely contraindicated.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked D (GB).

stem: 24-year-old obese woman, no previous pregnancy, complains of irregular menstrual periods. Menarche was at age of 14 and her periods were irregular in timing, duration and flow. The last menstrual flow was scanty 3 months ago. History of weight gain since menarche along with facial acne and mild facial hirsutism (see lab results). Test Result / Normal Values: Testosterone: 3.4 (0.7–2.8); Sex hormone-binding globulin: 9 (13–17); Luteinizing hormone (LH): 31 (5–22); Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH): 2.1 (5–20); Random Glucose: 6.1 (3.9–5.5). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: facial acne and mild facial hirsutism
why_right: She has irregular cycles since menarche, obesity with weight gain, acne and hirsutism (clinical hyperandrogenism), high testosterone with low SHBG (biochemical hyperandrogenism) and an LH:FSH ratio far above 3:1 (31 vs 2.1). The raised glucose fits PCOS-related insulin resistance. Oligo-anovulation plus hyperandrogenism already meets 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria.
why_wrong_block:
A. Turner syndrome causes primary amenorrhea, short stature and HIGH FSH from gonadal dysgenesis; she had menarche at 14 and her FSH is low.
B. Simple (exogenous) obesity can disturb cycles but does not explain the raised testosterone, low SHBG and the high LH:FSH ratio.
C. Premature ovarian failure gives secondary amenorrhea with HIGH FSH and LH and low estrogen (menopausal picture), not low FSH with hyperandrogenism.
key_concept:
PCOS = 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria (after excluding mimics):
  • Oligo or anovulation
  • Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
  • Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
  • Supportive: LH:FSH about 3:1 or more, low SHBG
  • Workup also: glucose tolerance and lipid profile
exam_pearl: Low FSH points away from ovarian failure and Turner (both have HIGH FSH); high LH with low FSH plus androgens is PCOS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked D (MG).

stem: 47-year-old woman with large symptomatic uterine fibroid, heavy menstrual bleeding. Completed childbearing. Significant comorbidities: uncontrolled DM and OSA. Prefers non-surgical management.
why_right: She has a large symptomatic fibroid with heavy bleeding, has completed childbearing, is a poor surgical candidate (uncontrolled DM and OSA raise anaesthetic and wound risk) and prefers non-surgical management. Uterine artery embolization is the minimally invasive, durable option for a woman who declines or is unfit for surgery: it devascularises the fibroid, shrinking it and reducing bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. GnRH agonists shrink fibroids only temporarily, cause menopausal symptoms and bone loss so are limited to short courses, and the fibroid regrows on stopping; they are mainly used before surgery.
C. Hysterectomy is the definitive cure for a woman with completed family and large fibroids, but she prefers to avoid surgery and her comorbidities increase operative risk.
D. Myomectomy is the fertility-sparing surgical option for women who want future pregnancy; she has completed childbearing and wants a non-surgical route.
key_concept:
Fibroid management ladder:
  • Asymptomatic: observe, annual ultrasound
  • Symptom control: OCP, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid, LNG-IUS if cavity normal
  • GnRH agonist: short-term, preoperative shrinkage
  • Refuses or unfit for surgery: uterine artery embolization
  • Large (>7 cm) or failed medical: myomectomy (wants fertility) or hysterectomy (family complete)
exam_pearl: "Prefers non-surgical" plus significant comorbidities flips the answer from hysterectomy to UAE.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. Physical examination reveals normal breast development but absent pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Primary amenorrhea with normal breast development but absent pubic and axillary hair is the classic picture of complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY). The testes make testosterone, which is aromatised to estrogen and drives breast growth, but non-functioning androgen receptors mean no pubic or axillary hair; Müllerian structures are absent because the testes secrete AMH, so there is no uterus and no menses.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRKH (46,XX with normal ovaries) gives primary amenorrhea with normal breasts AND normal pubic and axillary hair; absent hair rules it out.
C. Gonadal failure means no ovarian estrogen, so breasts do not develop (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with high FSH).
D. Turner syndrome is a form of gonadal dysgenesis: absent breast development, short stature, webbed neck, high FSH; breasts here are normal.
key_concept:
Primary amenorrhea by breasts and hair:
  • Breasts present + hair absent: androgen insensitivity (XY, high testosterone, blind vagina, no uterus)
  • Breasts present + hair normal + no uterus: MRKH (XX)
  • Breasts present + hair normal + uterus present: outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen, transverse septum)
  • Breasts absent + high FSH: gonadal failure / Turner
  • Breasts absent + low FSH: hypothalamic or pituitary cause
exam_pearl: Breasts need estrogen, pubic and axillary hair need androgen action: breasts without hair means the androgen receptor is not working.

stem: FEMALE AT 37 weeks, what is prerequisite of ECV?
why_right: Before an external cephalic version the fetus must be shown to be well, because a non reassuring fetal monitoring pattern is itself an exclusion criterion for ECV. So a period of CTG is run before the procedure (and repeated afterwards) to confirm a reactive, reassuring trace. At 37 weeks the gestational age is already right for ECV, so the remaining prerequisite among these options is fetal monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prolonged maternal fasting is not a requirement for ECV; the real preparation is CTG, ultrasound to confirm breech and placental site, consent, and availability of theatre in case of fetal compromise.
B. Dating is relevant only to know she is at term for ECV, and at 37 weeks that is already established; repeated early and late dating confirmation is not a prerequisite step.
key_concept:
ECV: confirm fetal wellbeing and exclude contraindications before attempting.
  • Before: CTG (reassuring), ultrasound for presentation and placental site, consent
  • After: repeat CTG; anti D if Rh negative
  • Contraindications: placenta praevia, multiple pregnancy, significant third trimester bleeding
  • Also: suspected IUGR, uteroplacental insufficiency, abnormal liquor, uterine malformation
  • Non reassuring fetal monitoring pattern = do not proceed
exam_pearl: The prerequisite is proof of fetal wellbeing (CTG), not fasting; a non reassuring trace cancels the ECV.

stem: 33-year-old nulliparous woman with cyclic pelvic pain and dyschezia underwent diagnostic laparoscopy. Most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Cyclic pelvic pain (dysmenorrhea) plus dyschezia in a nulliparous woman are classic Ds of endometriosis. Diagnostic laparoscopy is the confirmatory test and shows peritoneal implants, classically dark blue, black or brown "powder burn" lesions. Pain on defecation points to disease in the pouch of Douglas or rectovaginal septum.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic TB presents with infertility, constitutional symptoms and tubercles or adhesions at laparoscopy, not a cyclic pain pattern with dyschezia.
B. Adenomyosis is endometrium within the myometrium, giving a diffusely enlarged boggy uterus with menorrhagia, typically in older multiparous women; it is not seen as peritoneal implants and does not explain dyschezia.
D. PID gives fever, discharge, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness with non cyclic pain; it would be right with an acute infective picture.
key_concept:
Endometriosis = endometrial tissue outside the uterus (ovary most common site).
  • 3 Ds: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia; plus infertility
  • Exam: normal sized, fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity
  • Initial test: TVUS (endometrioma = ground glass cyst)
  • Confirmatory: laparoscopy with biopsy
  • Adenomyosis instead: enlarged boggy uterus + menorrhagia, multiparous
exam_pearl: Normal sized uterus + dyschezia = endometriosis; enlarged boggy uterus + heavy bleeding = adenomyosis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presented to the clinic unsure of her gestational age. She missed her period 3 months ago but her periods are irregular. Ultrasound: determined gestational age as 11 weeks. Which of the following was measured in the ultrasound to determine gestational age?
why_right: A gestational age of "11 weeks" is in the first trimester, where the dating parameter is the crown-rump length. CRL is used up to 13+6 weeks and is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy when the LMP is unknown or cycles are irregular.
why_wrong_block:
A. Femur length is a second and third trimester biometric parameter, not used for first-trimester dating.
C. Abdominal circumference is used after 13+6 weeks and is the most sensitive parameter for fetal growth and weight, not for first-trimester dating.
D. BPD and head circumference are the dating parameters after the first trimester (from about 14 weeks), not at 11 weeks.
key_concept:
Match the ultrasound parameter to the trimester.
  • Up to 13+6 weeks: crown-rump length (dating)
  • Second trimester dating: BPD and head circumference
  • Growth and estimated fetal weight: abdominal circumference (most sensitive)
  • Femur length: part of later biometry
exam_pearl: First trimester dating = CRL; a question about fetal growth restriction late in pregnancy = abdominal circumference.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second Trimester → D; Third Trimester → C.

stem: Female with vulvar pain. On examination there is an ulcer in the labia minora with ragged edges, necrotic center, and regional lymphadenopathy (picture provided). What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ulcer in the labia minora with ragged edges, necrotic center
why_right: A painful vulvar ulcer with ragged edges, a necrotic base and tender regional lymphadenopathy is the textbook picture of chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The inguinal nodes may suppurate into buboes. Painful ulcers point to chancroid or herpes; the ragged necrotic single ulcer favours chancroid.
why_wrong_block:
B. HIV is not a cause of this classic ulcer; acute HIV gives fever, rash and generalized lymphadenopathy. Chancroid does increase HIV transmission, so testing is advised, but it is not the diagnosis.
C. Herpes zoster gives painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal band, not a single ragged necrotic ulcer; for genital vesicles that erode into multiple shallow painful ulcers think herpes simplex.
key_concept:
Genital ulcer: decide by pain first.
  • Painful + ragged, necrotic + tender nodes: chancroid (H. ducreyi)
  • Painful + multiple shallow vesicles/ulcers: HSV
  • Painless, clean base, indurated + non tender nodes: primary syphilis
  • Painless + tender inguinal nodes: LGV (Chlamydia L1 to L3)
  • Painless beefy red bleeding ulcer, no nodes: granuloma inguinale
exam_pearl: Painful ones contain "H": Haemophilus ducreyi and Herpes; a painless ulcer flips it to syphilis.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with a history of involuntary urine leak, especially when she runs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next clinical evaluation?
highlight_terms_source: involuntary urine leak, especially when she runs
why_right: Leakage when she runs (exertion raising intra-abdominal pressure) is stress urinary incontinence. The bedside clinical test that demonstrates and confirms it is the cough stress test: leakage is seen at the urethral meatus with coughing on a full bladder.
why_wrong_block:
A. The Q-tip test only assesses urethral hypermobility; it does not demonstrate the leak and is not the standard confirmatory test.
C. The Bonney (bladder neck elevation) test was used to predict surgical success; it is outdated and not the next evaluation.
D. Uroflowmetry measures voiding flow and is used for voiding dysfunction or obstruction, not to confirm stress incontinence.
key_concept:
Incontinence workup:
  • Every patient: urinalysis or urine culture to exclude UTI
  • Stress (cough, sneeze, running): cough stress test
  • Urge: clinical diagnosis after excluding UTI; urodynamics (detrusor overactivity) only if mixed, unclear or refractory
  • Overflow: constant dribbling, weak stream, incomplete emptying
  • Stress treatment: pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises first, TVT definitive
exam_pearl: Leak with exertion = stress incontinence = cough stress test; urodynamics are not a first-line test for any type.

stem: lady who was diagnosed with ectopic pregnancy she lives far (The Mentioned Specific Distance) from the clinic and her vitals as follows: Bp 90/69 [NOT SURE], Hr 112 And bmi 31. What is the contraindications for mtx:
key_concept:
MTX for ectopic needs ALL criteria; instability = absolute contraindication.
  • Hemodynamically stable, no rupture
  • Beta hCG ≤5000 IU/L
  • No fetal cardiac activity
  • Mass <4 cm
  • Able to attend follow up (beta hCG day 4 and 7): distance = relative contraindication
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to The vital signs.
exam_pearl: "Absolute" points to instability (vitals); "favours surgery" in a stable patient points to social history and distance.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 24-year-old primigravida presents with the diagnosis of right ectopic pregnancy. The ultrasound revealed a 3 cm right tubal gestational sac with 5-week crown rump length, negative fetal heart activity and minimal amount of fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her social history reveals that she lives in a village 80 km away from the city center (see lab result). Blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Temperature 35.6 °C, BMI 36 kg/m², Human chorionic gonadotropin 3500. Which of the following would be the absolute contraindication to the use of methotrexate for this patient?
OptA: The B-hCG level and ultrasound findings
OptB: The far distance from medical services
why_right: BP 90/50 with HR 110 indicates hemodynamic instability, which suggests rupture and is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate. She needs surgical management after resuscitation. Everything else in the stem would actually allow medical treatment or is only relative. Minimal free fluid alone can occur in an unruptured ectopic; it is the vitals that make her unstable.
why_wrong_block:
A. hCG 3500 (≤5000), a 3 cm mass (<4 cm) and absent fetal heart activity all meet methotrexate criteria; these would contraindicate MTX only if hCG were above 5000, the mass ≥4 cm or cardiac activity present.
B. Living 80 km away limits follow up of serial beta hCG, which is a relative contraindication and favours surgery in a stable patient, but it is not absolute.
C. Obesity is not a contraindication to methotrexate; the dose is based on body surface area.
key_concept:
MTX criteria for ectopic (all needed):
  • Hemodynamically stable, unruptured
  • Beta hCG ≤5000 IU/L
  • No fetal cardiac activity
  • Mass <4 cm
  • Reliable follow up: beta hCG day 4 and day 7, expect >15% fall
  • Unstable or ruptured: surgery after stabilization
exam_pearl: Instability = absolute contraindication; distance from hospital = relative only.

stem: women had a baby through a success vaginal delivery. What are you going to do to prevent infection during post partum period ?
OptD: Frequent irrigation of the perineal area with special Sanitizers
highlight_terms_source: prevent infection during post partum period
why_right: After an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, the single most effective measure to prevent puerperal infection is hand hygiene by staff and the mother (before perineal care, pad changes and breastfeeding). Hands are the main route of cross transmission, the lesson behind puerperal sepsis prevention. Nothing in the stem calls for antibiotics or special perineal products.
why_wrong_block:
B. A sitz bath soothes perineal pain, a repaired episiotomy or hemorrhoids, but it is a comfort measure and does not prevent postpartum infection.
C. Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated after an uncomplicated vaginal birth; they are given for specific indications such as manual removal of the placenta or a third or fourth degree tear.
D. Frequent antiseptic irrigation of the perineum is unnecessary and can irritate tissue; simple perineal hygiene with clean water and regular pad changes is sufficient.
key_concept:
Infection prevention: hand hygiene is the single most important measure.
  • Uncomplicated vaginal birth: no routine antibiotics
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: manual removal of placenta, 3rd/4th degree tear, cesarean
  • Perineal care: clean water, frequent pad change, keep dry
  • Sitz bath: pain relief, not prophylaxis
exam_pearl: "Prevent infection" with no specific risk factor in the stem = hand washing, not antibiotics.

stem: A 41-year-old woman Para 4 presented to the Gynecology Clinic with post-coital bleeding for the past three months. Her cycle is irregular, and she is not taking any contraception. Examination revealed a soft abdomen with no palpable masses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Post-coital bleeding points to a cervical source (cervicitis, ectropion, polyp, dysplasia or cancer). With a normal abdomen, the first step is to examine the cervix and take a Pap smear to rule out cervical dysplasia or cancer; a visible lesion would go straight to colposcopy and biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Pelvic ultrasound assesses the uterus and adnexa (fibroids, endometrial thickness); it does not evaluate the cervix, the likely source here.
C. Endometrial biopsy is for heavy or intermenstrual AUB over 45 or postmenopausal bleeding; post-coital bleeding is a cervical clue, and at 41 it is not first.
D. D&C is an invasive endometrial procedure for severe refractory bleeding or failed office sampling; not the first step for a suspected cervical cause.
key_concept:
Source of genital bleeding guides the test.
  • Scanty post-coital bleeding: cervix, so speculum exam + Pap smear
  • Visible cervical lesion: colposcopy + biopsy
  • Heavy bleeding: uterus, so TVUS
  • AUB over 45 or postmenopausal: endometrial biopsy
exam_pearl: Post-coital = cervix; if the stem describes a visible cervical mass, skip the Pap and go to colposcopy + biopsy.

stem: 34 weeks gestation presents to ER with ROM.placenta was 1cm dilated.She delivers vaginally after 6hrs and with 2nd degree perineal tear.Placental Delivery was delayed and was removed manually. which of these indicates the reason of giving prophylactic antibiotics ?
why_right: Manual removal of the placenta means a hand is passed into the uterine cavity, introducing organisms and raising the risk of endometritis, so a single dose of prophylactic antibiotics is recommended. It is done under adequate analgesia or anesthesia with antibiotic cover. Of the events listed, it is the only recognized indication for postpartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
why_wrong_block:
A. A second degree tear (perineal muscles, sphincter intact) is simply repaired without routine antibiotics; prophylaxis is indicated for third and fourth degree tears involving the anal sphincter or rectal mucosa.
B. Six hours of ROM is not the trigger for antibiotics (prolonged ROM means ≥18 hours for GBS prophylaxis). Preterm labour <37 weeks with unknown GBS status is a separate intrapartum GBS indication, but the option names the ROM duration, which does not justify prophylaxis.
C. Precipitous labour (very rapid delivery, under about 3 hours) predisposes to tears and PPH, not to a need for antibiotic prophylaxis; and a 6 hour labour is not precipitous.
key_concept:
Antibiotic prophylaxis around vaginal birth is indication based.
  • Manual removal of placenta: yes
  • 3rd or 4th degree perineal tear: yes
  • 1st/2nd degree tear or episiotomy: no routine antibiotics
  • GBS intrapartum prophylaxis: ROM ≥18 h, GBS positive, prior GBS baby, fever
  • Retained placenta: wait 30 min, then manual removal, then D&C if tissue retained
exam_pearl: Any intrauterine manipulation (manual removal) earns antibiotic prophylaxis; a simple 2nd degree tear does not.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents at 29 weeks of gestation with prelabor premature rupture of membranes for 7 days. Examination revealed she is having lower abdominal pain, rigors, and fever with purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: prelabor premature rupture of membranes for 7 days
fever with purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge
why_right: Membranes ruptured 7 days ago (prolonged PPROM) give an ascending route for infection. Now fever, rigors, lower abdominal pain and purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge are the clinical picture of chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection).
why_wrong_block:
B. Urinary tract infection: causes dysuria, frequency or loin pain with fever; it does not produce purulent foul vaginal discharge after ruptured membranes.
C. Antepartum hemorrhage: presents with vaginal bleeding (painless in previa, painful in abruption), not fever with purulent discharge.
D. Lower respiratory tract infection: would give cough, dyspnea and chest signs, not abdominal pain with foul vaginal discharge.
key_concept:
Prolonged ROM + fever + uterine tenderness/abdominal pain + foul discharge = chorioamnionitis.
  • May also show maternal and fetal tachycardia
  • Treatment: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ampicillin + gentamicin) AND delivery
  • Tocolysis is contraindicated
  • Chorioamnionitis is an indication to end expectant PPROM management
exam_pearl: In PPROM, fever is chorioamnionitis until proven otherwise; the next step is antibiotics plus delivery, not tocolysis.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2284C).
Compiler note: Answer line reads: Chorioamnionitis (GB).

stem: Patient pregnant asthmatic and didn't have an attack for 6 months (implying controlled asthma). What is most likely to be progressively increasing during pregnancy?
why_right: In pregnancy, progesterone stimulates the respiratory centre, and minute ventilation rises mainly through a progressive increase in tidal volume, not respiratory rate. This produces a mild compensated respiratory alkalosis (lower PaCO2). A controlled asthmatic follows normal physiology, so tidal volume is what rises across gestation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Respiratory rate stays essentially unchanged in normal pregnancy; a raised rate in an asthmatic suggests an exacerbation, not physiology.
C. Reserve capacity does not rise: the enlarging uterus elevates the diaphragm, so expiratory reserve volume, residual volume and FRC fall, while inspiratory reserve stays roughly unchanged. Only tidal volume rises progressively.
key_concept:
Respiratory changes in pregnancy: more air per breath, same rate.
  • Increased: tidal volume, minute ventilation, oxygen consumption
  • Unchanged: respiratory rate, vital capacity, FEV1
  • Decreased: ERV, residual volume, FRC
  • Blood gas: lower PaCO2, mild compensated respiratory alkalosis
exam_pearl: Pregnancy raises ventilation by deeper breaths (tidal volume), never by faster breathing; FRC goes down.

stem: Patient single, sexually active. She has a problem remembering taking daily medications. She wants contraception that provides privacy and long-term protection.
why_right: She forgets daily medication and wants privacy and long term protection. The etonogestrel implant is a long acting reversible contraceptive inserted subdermally in the arm for several years, needs no daily action, is invisible to others and does not depend on a partner. LARC methods have the lowest failure rates because they remove user error.
why_wrong_block:
B. The OCP needs a pill every day, which fails precisely in a woman who forgets daily medication; it suits a motivated, adherent user.
C. A diaphragm must be inserted with each act of intercourse, has high typical use failure and offers no long term protection.
D. Condoms need use at every act and partner cooperation, with higher typical use failure; they are the right answer when STI protection is the goal, and can be added to an implant for dual protection.
key_concept:
Poor adherence + wants long term, discreet contraception = LARC.
  • LARC: etonogestrel implant, copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUD
  • Implant: progestogen only, discreet, no daily action
  • Daily or per act methods (OCP, diaphragm, condom) fail with poor adherence
  • Condom: only method here protecting against STIs
exam_pearl: "Forgets pills" + "privacy" = implant; if the stem stresses STI protection, the condom is added, not substituted.

stem: A 33-year-old woman, known case of low-lying placenta, presented at 35 weeks of gestation with mild vaginal bleeding at home. Examination revealed her vital signs are normal, and no more bleeding is noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: In antepartum bleeding the sequence is: ultrasound to localize the placenta, then CTG for fetal wellbeing, then management by maternal and fetal stability. She is a known case of low-lying placenta, so the placenta is already localized, and with normal vitals and no further bleeding, the next step is CTG.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ultrasound is the first step when placental site is unknown; here she is a known case, so it can be skipped at this point.
C. A biophysical profile is a second-line fetal test after a non-reassuring or equivocal CTG, not the immediate check after a bleed.
D. Umbilical artery Doppler is for surveillance of growth restriction or placental insufficiency, not acute bleeding from a low placenta.
key_concept:
Antepartum bleeding with suspected or known previa:
  • Never digital vaginal exam first
  • Unknown placental site: ultrasound first
  • Known previa: CTG next
  • Then manage by stability and gestation
  • <37 weeks and stable: admit, steroids <34, MgSO4 <32, cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
exam_pearl: 'Known case' is the clue that removes ultrasound from first place.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem given as a screenshot (numbered 0514 in its source file, 'Answer: A'); compiler's line: Answer: CTG.

stem: Endometriosis. Most definitive management?
why_right: Endometriosis is estrogen dependent ectopic endometrial tissue, so the definitive treatment removes both the uterus and the source of estrogen: total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with excision of visible disease. It is reserved for severe or refractory disease in a woman who has completed her family. Earlier steps are medical treatment and then laparoscopic ablation or excision.
why_wrong_block: B. Endometrial ablation destroys only the lining inside the uterus to treat heavy menstrual bleeding; endometriosis lies outside the uterus, so ablation does not treat it.
key_concept:
Endometriosis treatment ladder:
  • First line medical: combined OCP or progestogen
  • Second line: levonorgestrel IUD
  • Medical failure: laparoscopic ablation or excision (fertility sparing)
  • Endometrioma: laparoscopic cystectomy, not aspiration
  • Definitive: TAH + BSO when family is complete
exam_pearl: Definitive must remove the ovaries too; hysterectomy alone leaves estrogen to drive residual disease.

stem: Pregnant woman G…P… 38 weeks of gestation presents with (labour pain I think, not so sure), breech presentation, 1 cm dilated cervix, she has AFI of 3 (they implied oligohydramnios but didn't say it). She requested ECV. Absolute contraindication for ECV?
why_right: An AFI of 3 means oligohydramnios, and abnormal amniotic fluid volume is on the exclusion list for external cephalic version. With little liquor there is no cushion to rotate the fetus, so version is less likely to succeed and more likely to cause cord compression or placental injury. Of the three options, it is the only true contraindication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Breech presentation is the indication for ECV, not a contraindication; the whole point of ECV is to turn a breech to cephalic.
C. Being in early labour with intact membranes (cervix only 1 cm) does not exclude ECV by itself. Ruptured membranes, an abnormal CTG or advanced labour would.
key_concept:
ECV is offered for breech from about 36 to 37 weeks unless an exclusion criterion is present.
  • Placenta praevia / low lying placenta
  • Abnormal amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios)
  • Non-reassuring CTG, suspected IUGR, uteroplacental insufficiency
  • Significant third-trimester bleeding
  • Multiple pregnancy, major uterine malformation
  • Uncontrolled hypertension / PIH, maternal cardiac disease, major fetal anomaly
exam_pearl: The malpresentation itself is never the contraindication; look for the ultrasound finding (low AFI, low placenta) or a bad CTG.

stem: 15 years old Turner (45 X) they didn't mention Turner, only the karyotype. She presented with no breast development and high FSH and LH and low estradiol. What do we give her?
OptB: Growth hormone only (they literally said only)
highlight_terms_source: high FSH and LH and low estradiol
why_right: A 45,X karyotype with absent breast development, high FSH/LH and low estradiol is Turner syndrome with streak gonads (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). The ovaries will not recover, so puberty must be induced with estrogen replacement, started at low dose and increased gradually, with progestogen added later to allow cyclic bleeding. At 15 years she is already late, and estrogen is also needed to protect bone and allow feminisation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Growth hormone treats Turner short stature, but it does nothing for the ovarian failure; giving it only leaves her without puberty and at risk of osteoporosis.
C. Observation is for constitutional delay, where gonadotropins are low and puberty will come. Here FSH/LH are high, meaning permanent ovarian failure, so waiting only delays treatment.
key_concept:
Delayed puberty: check FSH/LH first.
  • High FSH/LH + low estradiol = primary ovarian failure (Turner) = estrogen replacement
