  • Low FSH/LH = central cause or constitutional delay
  • Turner: GH for height, estrogen for puberty and bone; both may be used, not GH alone
  • Karyotype confirms Turner (45,X or mosaic)
exam_pearl: Turner with no breasts needs estrogen; growth hormone fixes height, not puberty.

stem: 33 years old patient with amenorrhea for 8 months. FSH 60 (high), LH 60 (high), prolactin normal, TSH normal. What is she at increased risk of?
why_right: Eight months of amenorrhea with FSH 60 and LH 60 and normal prolactin and TSH at age 33 is premature ovarian insufficiency. The ovaries no longer make estrogen, and estrogen deficiency accelerates bone loss, so osteoporosis is the main long-term risk. This is why POI is treated with HRT until the usual age of menopause.
why_wrong_block: B. Endometrial cancer is driven by unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity, estrogen-only HRT with a uterus). POI is a low estrogen state, so the endometrium is thin, not stimulated.
key_concept:
POI = ovarian failure before 40: high FSH/LH, low estrogen, amenorrhea.
  • FSH above about 45 suggests menopause; at a young age call it POI
  • Complications: osteoporosis, cardiovascular risk, vasomotor symptoms, infertility
  • Management: HRT to protect bone and relieve symptoms
  • High estrogen states (PCOS, obesity) instead raise endometrial cancer risk
exam_pearl: Low estrogen = bone loss; unopposed estrogen = endometrial cancer. Decide which hormonal state the labs show.

stem: Pregnant 30 w with mild bleeding?
why_right: At 30 weeks with mild bleeding the mother is stable and delivery may be needed within days, so the priority is admission and an antenatal corticosteroid course to mature the fetal lungs (given below 34 weeks). This is the standard expectant management of mild antepartum bleeding such as placenta praevia before term.
why_wrong_block:
B. Tocolytics are given only in preterm labour (regular contractions with cervical change), mainly to buy time for steroids. Bleeding without contractions does not need one, and tocolysis is generally avoided with active bleeding.
C. Antibiotics are indicated for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes or GBS prophylaxis in preterm labour; mild bleeding alone is not an infection indication.
key_concept:
Antepartum bleeding before 37 weeks: stability decides.
  • Severe bleeding or fetal distress: stabilise and deliver by caesarean
  • Mild bleeding: admit, steroids if below 34 weeks, magnesium sulfate if below 32 weeks and delivery is likely
  • Tocolytic only with contractions and cervical change
  • Placenta praevia: planned caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
exam_pearl: No contractions means no tocolytic; below 34 weeks with any threat of delivery, steroids come first.

stem: Female presented to clinic complaining of infertility for 4 years. Normal labs. Pic shows bilateral tube blockage. What is the most likely diagnosis according to X-ray pic?
why_right: The film is a hysterosalpingogram, and bilateral tubal blockage in a woman with 4 years of infertility and normal labs is the picture of hydrosalpinx: dye fills distended, dilated tubes that end blindly with no free spill into the peritoneum. Distal tubal occlusion, usually after PID, is the classic HSG cause of tubal factor infertility.
why_wrong_block:
B. An ovarian cyst is not outlined by HSG contrast; it is diagnosed on pelvic ultrasound and does not block the tubes.
C. Peritubal adhesions show loculated or pooled spill around a patent tube rather than a dilated blocked tube; they are confirmed at laparoscopy.
key_concept:
Tubal factor workup: HSG first, laparoscopy and dye to confirm.
  • Dilated blind-ending tubes, no spill = hydrosalpinx
  • Loculated spill around the tube = peritubal adhesions
  • Dark peritoneal spots at laparoscopy = endometriosis
  • Confirmed unilateral block: ovulation induction; bilateral block: IVF
exam_pearl: HSG with swollen tubes and no spill = hydrosalpinx; a laparoscopy image with dark spots = endometriosis.

stem: A 19-year-old G1 P0 at 42 weeks is admitted for induction of labor. Her antenatal care was uncomplicated. Examination revealed the cervix was closed and long. Prostaglandin E2 is placed vaginally. An hour later, she started to contract regularly, and the fetal heart dropped to 70 bpm and was not recovering. Her vaginal examination showed a fully dilated cervix and presenting part at +2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptD: Start pushing and consider applying ventouse
highlight_terms_source: fetal heart dropped to 70 bpm and was not recovering
why_right: A fetal heart at "70 bpm and not recovering" is prolonged bradycardia that demands immediate delivery. The decisive clue is "fully dilated cervix and presenting part at +2": the head is low enough for safe instrumental delivery, so the fastest route is pushing with ventouse assistance. The rapid change after PGE2 suggests uterine hyperstimulation, so the pessary should also be removed and in utero resuscitation started while delivery is expedited.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin increases contractions and would worsen hyperstimulation and fetal hypoxia; it is for slow progress with a reassuring fetal heart, not fetal distress.
B. The wording is unclear (fundal pressure or simply encouraging her); no manoeuvre replaces expedited operative delivery in a persistently bradycardic fetus.
C. Caesarean section is the route when the cervix is not fully dilated or the head is high; at full dilatation with the head at +2, instrumental delivery is faster and safer.
key_concept:
Fetal distress not responding to resuscitation: deliver by the fastest safe route.
  • Cervix not fully dilated: caesarean section
  • Fully dilated, head at +2 or lower: instrumental (ventouse or forceps) delivery
  • Fully dilated but head high: caesarean section
  • After PGE2 with tachysystole: remove the prostaglandin, consider tocolysis, left lateral position, fluids
  • Never start oxytocin in fetal distress
exam_pearl: Same bradycardia after PGE2 with a closed cervix is caesarean section; fully dilated at +2 flips it to ventouse.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: D (GB).

stem: A 30-year-old woman with primary infertility for the last 3 years is seen for follow-up in the clinic. Her investigations included a hormonal profile, and an ultrasound is normal. Her husband's semen analysis is also normal. She had a 3-month trial of induction of ovulation with clomiphene. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: husband's semen analysis is also normal
3-month trial of induction of ovulation with clomiphene
why_right: Male factor is excluded (normal semen analysis), and ovarian and uterine factors look normal (normal hormonal profile and ultrasound). She has also had a 3-month clomiphene trial without conceiving. The one factor never assessed is the tubes, so the next step is tubal patency testing, here by diagnostic laparoscopy (with dye).
why_wrong_block:
A. IVF is the treatment for confirmed bilateral tubal blockage or failed lower-level treatment. Jumping to it skips the tubal assessment.
C. IUI needs at least one patent tube, so the tubes must be assessed before it is offered.
D. Ovulation is not the problem (normal hormones, already tried clomiphene). Escalating to gonadotropins ignores the unassessed tubal factor.
key_concept:
Infertility work-up order:
  • Semen analysis (male) first
  • Ovulation: mid-luteal (day 21) progesterone, hormonal profile
  • Uterus and ovaries: ultrasound
  • Tubes: HSG (initial), laparoscopy and dye (confirmatory)
  • Treat by the factor found
exam_pearl: Before any assisted reproduction, the tubes must have been checked. If the stem never mentions them, assess the tubes.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (Gameboy).

stem: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. Urine osmolality is elevated >500 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely etiology for his acute kidney injury?
why_right: Excessive military training causes volume loss, and postural hypotension confirms hypovolemia. A urine osmolality > 500 means the tubules are intact and concentrating urine maximally, which defines pre-renal azotemia.
why_wrong_block:
B. AIN is intrinsic renal injury; damaged tubules cannot concentrate, so urine osmolality is low (< 300), and it usually follows a drug.
C. Glomerulonephritis is intrinsic renal disease with hematuria, RBC casts, edema and hypertension rather than postural hypotension.
D. ATN can follow prolonged hypovolemia, but tubular damage gives dilute urine (< 300) and FeNa > 2%; a concentrated urine means the tubules still work.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic AKI indices:
  • Urine osmolality: > 500 pre-renal; < 300 intrinsic
  • FeNa: < 1% pre-renal; > 2% ATN
  • Urine Na: low pre-renal; high ATN
  • BUN:Cr: > 20 pre-renal
  • Sediment: bland pre-renal; muddy brown casts ATN
exam_pearl: Concentrated urine (> 500) = tubules working = pre-renal; if exertion also gave dark urine and high CK, think rhabdomyolysis.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 3× in this file (also AS-1417B, AS-2501).

stem: 70 year-old female known case of DM, HTN and dyslipidemia admitted to stroke unit after presenting with ischemic stroke 2 days ago and was managed by anti platelets and physiotherapy, now he is presenting with fatigue VITAL SIGNS WERE NORMAL (literally mentioned like this) All labs were normal EXCEPT RBS was 12.6 what is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Two days after an ischemic stroke the patient is stable with normal vitals and the only abnormal result is a random glucose of 12.6 mmol/L. Hyperglycemia after acute stroke is linked with larger infarcts and worse outcomes, so it should be treated with insulin to bring glucose into the target range (roughly 7.8 to 10 mmol/L). Insulin is the only option that addresses the abnormal finding.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation would accept persistent hyperglycemia in an acute stroke patient, which worsens neurological outcome; observation fits only when glucose is already in target.
B. Warfarin is for cardioembolic stroke such as atrial fibrillation; none is described, and non-cardioembolic stroke uses antiplatelets, which he already receives.
D. tPA must be given within 4.5 hours of onset; at 2 days the window has long passed and the problem now is glucose, not a new occlusion.
key_concept:
After acute ischemic stroke: control the risk factors and avoid secondary injury.
  • tPA only within 4.5 hours, after CT excludes bleed
  • Aspirin from 24 to 48 hours; add clopidogrel short term when indicated
  • Anticoagulation only for a cardioembolic source (e.g. AF)
  • Treat hyperglycemia with insulin; avoid hypoglycemia
  • Control BP, diabetes and lipids (statin)
exam_pearl: Glucose above about 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) after a stroke is treated, not observed; aim for 7.8 to 10 and avoid hypoglycaemia (intensive IV control has no extra benefit over standard insulin control).

stem: Old patient with DM and CKD and intermittent claudication (no symptoms of heart failure or chest pain) Echo normal All normal values Presented complaining of atrial fibrillation How to control ventricular rate (written like this)
why_right: This recall's key is diltiazem. Stable AF with a normal echo and no heart failure is rate controlled with a beta blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. The source then uses the intermittent claudication to steer away from beta blockers (classic teaching that beta blockade can worsen peripheral vasoconstriction), and diltiazem is neutral or mildly vasodilating, so it is chosen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Digoxin is renally cleared and toxic in CKD, and it controls rate poorly during activity; it is preferred when AF coexists with heart failure or low blood pressure.
B. Losartan is an antihypertensive ARB with no effect on AV node conduction, so it does not control ventricular rate.
C. Metoprolol is a first-line rate control drug and would be equally good with normal EF; the source excluded it only because of the peripheral arterial disease.
key_concept:
AF rate control: pick by comorbidity.
  • Normal EF: beta blocker or diltiazem/verapamil
  • HFrEF: beta blocker or digoxin; avoid non-DHP CCB
  • Asthma / PAD (exam teaching): diltiazem
  • CKD: avoid digoxin if possible
  • Pre-excited AF (WPW): avoid AV nodal blockers
exam_pearl: Exam logic: AF + claudication = diltiazem; AF + heart failure = beta blocker or digoxin, never diltiazem.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Avoid beta blocker in PAD. AF with no HF and normal echo: first-line rate control is beta-blocker (metoprolol) or non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil). In PAD/Raynaud/severe claudication avoid beta-blockers: beta2 blockade reduces vasodilation, unopposed alpha vasoconstriction worsens claudication. Metoprolol is beta1-selective and often safe in real life, but in board-style AF + PAD prefer diltiazem (neutral/mild vasodilator). Table: normal EF BB or diltiazem; HFrEF beta-blocker; PAD diltiazem; CKD avoid digoxin if possible; WPW avoid AV nodal blockers. So answer = Diltiazem.
Other marked answers: C. Metoprolol (light highlight)

stem: A 60-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension and intermitent claudicaion due is diagnosed to have stable angina. Decision is made to manage him with intensive medical therapy. He is started on aspirin, rosuvastain and nitroglycerine but sill gets angina with moderate exercise. Blood pressure 130/85 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Which of the following is the most appropriate additional drug?
why_right: This recall's key is diltiazem. On aspirin, statin and nitrate he still has angina and a heart rate of 86, so a rate-limiting anti-anginal is needed to cut myocardial oxygen demand. The source avoids the beta blocker because of the intermittent claudication, and among the calcium channel blockers only diltiazem lowers heart rate as well as dilating the coronaries.
why_wrong_block:
B. Nifedipine, especially short acting, causes reflex tachycardia and can worsen angina; it should be combined with a beta blocker if used at all.
C. Amlodipine relieves angina by vasodilation but does not slow the heart rate, which is the problem here at 86/min; it is the CCB to add on top of a beta blocker.
D. Metoprolol is standard first-line therapy for stable angina; the source rejected it only because of the claudication.
key_concept:
Stable angina anti-anginal choice.
  • First line: beta blocker or rate-limiting CCB, plus sublingual nitrate
  • Beta blocker not tolerated or (exam) PAD/asthma: diltiazem or verapamil
  • Adding to a beta blocker: use a dihydropyridine (amlodipine), never verapamil
  • Avoid short-acting nifedipine alone: reflex tachycardia
exam_pearl: Rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem) replaces a beta blocker; a dihydropyridine (amlodipine) is added to one.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Listed under 11 as a related question (PAD/claudication -> prefer diltiazem over beta-blocker).

stem: 55 year old woman with DM HTN CKD with eGFR 50/ml/min. What is the goal BP to prevent cardiovascular disease?
highlight_terms_source: goal BP to prevent cardiovascular disease
why_right: She has diabetes, hypertension and CKD (eGFR 50), and cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in CKD. The source keys the strictest target, <125/70, following KDIGO, which recommends aiming for a systolic below 120 mmHg when tolerated because intensive control (SPRINT data) reduced cardiovascular events and overall mortality. Among the options, D is the only one in line with that intensive target.
why_wrong_block:
A. <155/100 is far above any treatment target and would leave her in the hypertensive range.
B. <145/90 is closer to the old relaxed target for the elderly and is too loose for a high-risk patient with diabetes and CKD.
C. <135/80 is near the older diabetes/CKD target (about 130/80, still used by ACC/AHA and ADA), but the source prefers the more intensive KDIGO systolic goal.
key_concept:
BP targets in high-risk patients.
  • KDIGO CKD: systolic below 120 if tolerated (standardised measurement)
  • ACC/AHA and ADA: below 130/80
  • ACE inhibitor/ARB first line in diabetes with CKD or albuminuria
  • Intensive control: watch for AKI, hypotension, falls
exam_pearl: In recalls, diabetes + CKD + 'prevent cardiovascular disease' points to the strictest target offered (KDIGO systolic below 120).

KDIGO guidelines state target <120 is associated with more cardio protection (although it might have more risk of AKI, overall people with more strict control have less overall mortality); based on SPRINT. stem: Patient K/C of HTN, diagnosed as TB and started on 1st line Anti-TB medications, he is on Lisinopril and Amlodipine for HTN, what is the most appropriate adjustment for his medications?
why_right: This recall's key is to increase the lisinopril dose. The reasoning is that rifampicin, part of first-line anti-TB therapy, is a strong enzyme inducer that lowers amlodipine levels, so blood pressure control may slip; the source compensates by uptitrating the other agent rather than stopping either drug or the rifampicin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping amlodipine would remove one of his two antihypertensives and worsen control; the interaction is managed by monitoring and adjusting dose, not stopping.
B. Rifampicin is a core first-line TB drug; interactions are handled by adjusting the other medicines, not by dropping rifampicin.
C. Lowering lisinopril makes no sense: rifampicin reduces the effect of his antihypertensive regimen, so BP is more likely to rise, not fall.
key_concept:
Rifampicin = potent liver enzyme (CYP) inducer: it lowers levels of many co-drugs.
  • Warfarin: increase dose, monitor INR closely
  • Amlodipine and other CYP3A4 drugs: effect falls, monitor BP and adjust
  • Hormonal contraception: becomes unreliable
  • Rifampicin is kept and the co-drug adjusted (rare exceptions such as some HIV regimens, where rifabutin is substituted)
exam_pearl: In rifampicin interaction questions, adjust the affected drug rather than stopping rifampicin.

⚠ Debated: Compiler highlights D, but a 'Sofyan note' directly below says 'The correct: Increase Amlodipine dose', which is not among the options; page endorsement contested.
Compiler note: Sofyan note: The correct Increase Amlodipine dose.
Other marked answers: Sofyan note: Increase Amlodipine dose (not among options)

stem: Elderly Male On Amlodipine, Beta Blocker, And Lisinopril Presents With Flu-Like Symptoms. Acid-Fast Bacilli Result Came Positive, And He Was Started On First-Line Anti-TB Regimen. Which Antihypertensive Drug Should Be Stopped?
why_right: First-line anti-TB therapy includes rifampicin, a potent inducer of hepatic CYP3A4. Amlodipine is cleared by CYP3A4, so its levels fall markedly and BP control can be lost; it is the drug in this list that needs dose adjustment or a switch. The same induction logic explains why warfarin doses must rise when rifampicin is started.
why_wrong_block:
B. Beta blocker: interaction with rifampicin is minor and not the classic one tested; it is the drug to watch in asthma (bronchospasm) or in bradycardia, not with TB drugs.
C. Lisinopril: excreted unchanged by the kidney, not hepatically metabolised, so rifampicin induction does not affect it. It would need adjusting for hyperkalaemia or worsening renal function.
key_concept:
Rifampicin = strong CYP3A4 inducer: lowers levels of drugs cleared by the liver.
  • Amlodipine and other dihydropyridine CCBs: reduced effect
  • Warfarin: dose must be increased
  • Oral contraceptives: fail, use another method
  • Steroids, many antiretrovirals, azoles: reduced levels
  • Renally cleared drugs (ACE inhibitors) are unaffected
exam_pearl: When TB treatment starts, ask which co-drug is hepatically (CYP3A4) cleared: that one needs adjustment, not the renally cleared ACE inhibitor.

stem: 43 years old man presented to the ER complaining of Lower limb weakness and urine incontinence and difficulty walking since 3 days, T10 sensory level no history of previous infection mentioned. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Lower limb weakness and urine incontinence
why_right: A T10 sensory level with lower limb weakness and urinary incontinence localises the lesion to the thoracic spinal cord (myelopathy), not the peripheral nerves. With a subacute 3 day course and no preceding infection, the recall's key is extrinsic spinal cord compression (disc, tumour/metastasis, abscess, haematoma), which is the emergency to exclude first with urgent whole spine MRI.
why_wrong_block:
B. Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending weakness with areflexia after an infection, without a sharp sensory level and with sphincters usually spared early; a sensory level points to the cord, not nerves.
C. Transverse myelitis: also gives a sensory level and bladder involvement, but is typically post-infectious or linked to MS, NMO or SLE; it is a diagnosis made after MRI excludes compression.
D. Cauda equina syndrome: lesion below L1 with saddle anaesthesia and lower motor neuron signs; it cannot produce a thoracic (T10) sensory level.
key_concept:
Sensory level + sphincter dysfunction = spinal cord lesion until proven otherwise.
  • Compression: most common and surgically urgent; urgent MRI whole spine
  • Transverse myelitis: post-infectious, MS, NMO, SLE; MRI then LP
  • GBS: ascending, areflexia, no sensory level, CSF high protein
  • Cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, LMN signs, below L1
exam_pearl: Recent viral illness or autoimmune disease with a sensory level tilts to transverse myelitis; no trigger, back pain or known cancer tilts to compression.

stem: A patient with Burkit Lymphoma (DLBCL In Another Recall) is receiving B-CHOP chemotherapy. Laboratory results show hyperkalemia (6) and hypocalcemia. (Unable to urinate) What is the most appropriate management (in addition to hydration)? Uric Acid Not Mentioned
why_right: Chemotherapy for a high grade lymphoma (Burkitt, DLBCL) followed by hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia and being unable to urinate is established tumour lysis syndrome with acute kidney injury. Alongside aggressive hydration, rasburicase rapidly breaks down existing uric acid, protecting the kidneys from urate nephropathy; it is preferred over allopurinol in established or high risk TLS, especially with AKI, even though the uric acid level is not stated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lasix: only added for volume overload once the patient is adequately hydrated; it does not treat the cause and can worsen renal injury in a dry patient.
B. Thiazide: no role in TLS; it raises uric acid and calcium reabsorption and is used for hypercalciuric stones or hypertension instead.
key_concept:
TLS = high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, LOW calcium, AKI after starting chemotherapy.
  • Highest risk: Burkitt, bulky DLBCL, ALL, high tumour burden
  • All patients: aggressive IV hydration
  • Established TLS or high risk: rasburicase
  • Intermediate risk or rasburicase unavailable: allopurinol
  • Refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguria, severe AKI: dialysis
exam_pearl: Established TLS with AKI: rasburicase lowers uric acid that is already there; allopurinol only blocks new production.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Highly suggestive of acute Tumor Lysis Syndrome with acute kidney injury. According to UpToDate and oncology guidelines: Rasburicase is preferred over allopurinol in established or high-risk TLS, especially with AKI.

stem: 50 yo male newly diagnosed with BULKY diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), came to ER c/o N& V, decreased urine output for 24 h after first cycle of chemotherapy (R CHOP) K 6 P04-3 Ca 1.2 UA 570 What is the drug that help in PREVENT such presentation?
highlight_terms_source: BULKY diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
why_right: Bulky DLBCL starting R-CHOP is high risk for tumour lysis syndrome, and this patient developed it (K 6, high phosphate, low Ca, UA 570, falling urine output). For high risk patients the prophylactic drug of choice, given with hydration before chemotherapy, is rasburicase, which converts uric acid to soluble allantoin and lowers levels rapidly.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thiazide: raises serum uric acid and has no role in TLS prevention; it is used to reduce calcium stone formation in hypercalciuria.
B. Allopurinol: prevents new uric acid formation and is the choice for intermediate risk or when rasburicase is not offered, but it does not clear existing urate in a high risk, bulky tumour.
D. Prednisone: part of the R-CHOP regimen itself and lymphocytolytic, so it contributes to lysis rather than preventing TLS.
key_concept:
TLS prophylaxis by risk.
  • Low risk: hydration, monitoring
  • Intermediate risk: hydration + allopurinol
  • High risk (Burkitt, bulky DLBCL, ALL with high WBC): hydration + rasburicase
  • Rasburicase contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis)
exam_pearl: If rasburicase is listed it wins for a bulky high grade lymphoma; if it is absent, allopurinol is the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: See 31c: when Rasburicase is not among the options, Allopurinol is the answer.

stem: 50 yo male newly diagnosed with BULKY diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), came to ER c/o N& V, decreased urine output for 24 h after first cycle of chemotherapy (R CHOP) K 6 P04-3 Ca 1.2 UA 570 What is the drug that help in PREVENT such presentation? (No Rasburicase in options)
highlight_terms_source: BULKY diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
why_right: Same picture: bulky DLBCL after the first R-CHOP cycle with TLS (K 6, low Ca, UA 570, oliguria). The question asks which drug helps prevent it, and with rasburicase absent from the options, allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that blocks new uric acid production) given with hydration before chemotherapy is the correct preventive drug.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thiazide: increases serum uric acid and is for hypercalciuric stones or hypertension, not TLS prevention.
C. Blank option in this recall version; in the full version this slot is rasburicase, which is chosen whenever it is offered for a high risk tumour.
D. Prednisone: a component of R-CHOP that itself causes lymphocyte lysis, so it does not prevent TLS.
key_concept:
Uric acid lowering in TLS.
  • Allopurinol: blocks xanthine oxidase, prevents new urate; slower, intermediate risk
  • Rasburicase: degrades existing urate; fast, high risk or established TLS
  • Both given with aggressive IV hydration
exam_pearl: Read the options first: rasburicase listed means rasburicase; not listed means allopurinol.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No Rasburicase (option C blank in this version).

stem: A 58 year presents with progressive dyspnea dyspn and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Echo done: hypokinesia of anterior wall and left ventricle ejection fraction 30%. Which of the following is the next best investigation:
why_right: Dyspnoea and PND with an echo showing EF 30% and regional hypokinesia of the anterior wall means new heart failure with reduced EF whose regional pattern suggests an ischaemic cause (LAD territory). The next step is to define the coronary anatomy with coronary angiography, which confirms CAD and allows revascularisation planning, since ischaemic cardiomyopathy changes management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial perfusion: a non-invasive test for inducible ischaemia or viability in stable chest pain with intermediate probability; with an EF of 30% and a regional defect, definitive anatomy is needed.
B. CT angio: best for ruling out CAD in low to intermediate pretest probability; here ischaemic cardiomyopathy is likely and invasive angiography also allows intervention.
D. Chest x-ray: part of the initial workup for pulmonary oedema and cardiomegaly, but the diagnosis is already made by echo and it cannot identify the cause.
key_concept:
New HFrEF: find the cause.
  • Echo: confirms reduced EF and shows regional vs global dysfunction
  • Regional wall motion abnormality: think ischaemic, go to coronary angiography
  • Global hypokinesia, young, no risk factors: think dilated cardiomyopathy (viral, alcohol, familial)
  • Low to intermediate CAD probability: CT coronary angiography
exam_pearl: Regional hypokinesia on echo points to coronary disease; global hypokinesia points to a non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 50 year old male patient presented with recurrent chest tightness radiating to the shoulder, relieved after 4 minutes with rest. There is a family history of sudden death (his brother died suddenly at the age of 46). ECG shows left bundle branch block What is the most appropriate to assess the coronary arteries?
highlight_terms_source: ECG shows left bundle branch block
why_right: Exertional chest tightness relieved by rest in 4 minutes is typical stable angina. Normally the next test is exercise ECG, but left bundle branch block makes the ST segments uninterpretable, so the recall's key is a stress imaging test: myocardial perfusion imaging, ideally with pharmacological (vasodilator) stress to avoid false septal defects in LBBB.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT angio: anatomical test favoured for low to intermediate probability chest pain; the classic exam logic for LBBB is functional stress imaging rather than CT.
C. Exercise ECG: right when the resting ECG is normal and the patient can exercise; LBBB (also LVH, paced rhythm, WPW, digoxin) makes it non-diagnostic.
D. Calcium CT: a risk stratification tool for asymptomatic people, not a diagnostic test for symptomatic angina.
key_concept:
Stable chest pain testing.
  • Normal resting ECG, can exercise: exercise ECG (classic exam ladder)
  • Uninterpretable ECG (LBBB, paced, LVH, WPW, digoxin): stress imaging (perfusion or stress echo)
  • Cannot exercise: pharmacological stress imaging
  • Low to intermediate probability: CT coronary angiography
  • High probability or high risk result: invasive angiography
exam_pearl: LBBB on the resting ECG kills the exercise ECG option: move to stress imaging.

stem: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented to the Emergency Department with 3-hour continuous retrosternal heaviness associated with profuse sweating. Physical examination reveals tachycardia and an S4 gallop on heart auscultation. The patient is commenced on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin infusion (see reports). Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block. Previous ECG was normal. Cardiac enzymes: Pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Wait for the results of cardiac enzymes
highlight_terms_source: left bundle branch block. Previous ECG was normal
why_right: Ongoing "3-hour continuous retrosternal heaviness" with sweating in a diabetic hypertensive, plus a "left bundle branch block" when the "previous ECG was normal", is treated as a STEMI equivalent. Reperfusion must not wait for biomarkers, and among the options thrombolysis is the reperfusion therapy offered (primary PCI would be preferred if available promptly).
why_wrong_block:
A. Start lidocaine infusion: prophylactic antiarrhythmics are not given in MI; lidocaine is only for sustained ventricular arrhythmias.
B. Perform exercise ECG testing: contraindicated in an ongoing acute coronary syndrome; it is for stable chest pain evaluation.
D. Wait for cardiac enzymes: STEMI and its equivalents are ECG diagnoses; waiting for troponin delays reperfusion ("time is muscle"). Waiting is reasonable only for suspected NSTEMI/unstable angina without ST elevation.
key_concept:
STEMI or STEMI equivalent = reperfuse now, without waiting for enzymes.
  • STEMI equivalents: new LBBB with ischemic symptoms, posterior MI, Sgarbossa-positive LBBB
  • Primary PCI if available in time; otherwise thrombolysis
  • Thrombolysis benefit is greatest early after symptom onset
  • Initial: aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, nitrates, beta blocker if no contraindication
exam_pearl: "Previous ECG was normal" is the clue that makes the LBBB new and turns the case into a reperfusion question.

stem: Female on warfarin present with bloody stool, she is pale, hypotensive and has cool extremities. Her lab (Hb is 6, PTT and PT prolonged, BP is 90/65) What is the the appropriate step in fluid management?
why_right: This is major bleeding on warfarin (bloody stool, hypotension, cool extremities, Hb 6) with prolonged PT and PTT. Warfarin bleeding with symptoms means urgent reversal: IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP if PCC is unavailable), because volume replacement alone will not stop bleeding while the clotting factors are depleted. The recall's key focuses on correcting the coagulopathy driving the haemorrhage.
why_wrong_block:
A. RL: crystalloid restores volume briefly in shock but does not replace red cells or clotting factors and dilutes both further.
C. Normal saline: right for a hypotensive bleeder with Hb above the transfusion threshold and no coagulopathy; here bleeding continues while anticoagulated.
D. Packed RBC: needed for haemorrhagic shock with Hb 6 and given alongside reversal, but it does not reverse warfarin, which is what the key targets.
key_concept:
Warfarin and high INR algorithm.
  • Bleeding (any INR): admit, IV vitamin K + PCC (or FFP)
  • No bleeding, very high INR: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K
  • No bleeding, mildly high INR: hold or reduce dose, recheck
  • PCC preferred over FFP: faster, smaller volume
  • Hb below 7 or ongoing shock: transfuse packed RBC in parallel
exam_pearl: Bleeding on warfarin: vitamin K alone is too slow, so pair it with PCC (or FFP).

stem: A 65-Year-Old Female Patient Known Case Of CHD Due To Cardiomyopathy Came For Routine Follow-Up And Is Asymptomatic. BP 110/85 MmHg, HR 145 Irregular. ECG Showed Atrial Fibrillation (AF). What Is The Best Next Step In Management?
why_right: She is asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable (BP 110/85) with fast AF (HR 145) and known cardiomyopathy, so the priority is rate control, not cardioversion. In stable heart failure with reduced EF, a beta blocker such as bisoprolol controls the rate and also improves survival in HFrEF, which is why it is the recall's key.
why_wrong_block:
A. Verapamil: non-dihydropyridine CCBs are negatively inotropic and avoided in HFrEF; they are rate control choices when EF is preserved or beta blockers are contraindicated (e.g. asthma).
B. Digoxin: rate control for AF with heart failure when hypotensive, acutely decompensated or as an add-on to a beta blocker; it controls resting rate only and has no survival benefit.
D. Electrical cardioversion: right for haemodynamically unstable AF (hypotension, shock, ischaemia, acute pulmonary oedema); she is stable.
key_concept:
AF management fork.
  • Unstable: immediate electrical cardioversion
  • Stable: rate control, target HR below 100 (classic teaching)
  • Rate control options: beta blocker, CCB, digoxin
  • Stable HFrEF: beta blocker first; avoid verapamil and diltiazem
  • Acute decompensated HF or hypotension: digoxin (or amiodarone)
  • Always assess anticoagulation with CHA2DS2-VASc
exam_pearl: Stable AF with heart failure: beta blocker if compensated, digoxin if decompensated or hypotensive.

stem: In a patient with heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy presenting with fast atrial fibrillation, which of the following drugs is the most appropriate to control the heart rate?
why_right: The decisive clues are "heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy" plus "fast atrial fibrillation" and the lead-in "control the heart rate". In AF coexisting with heart failure, digoxin is the rate-control drug of choice because it slows AV conduction while being positively inotropic, so it does not depress an already weak ventricle.
why_wrong_block:
B. Diltiazem: a non-dihydropyridine CCB is negatively inotropic and is avoided in HF with reduced EF; it is a good rate-control choice in AF with normal LV function (e.g. AF with COPD/asthma or claudication).
C. Ivabradine: works on the sinus node If current, so it needs sinus rhythm; it does nothing for ventricular rate in AF. It is used in HFrEF patients in sinus rhythm with a persistently high heart rate.
D. Propranolol: a non-selective beta blocker without HF evidence; started acutely in a failing dilated ventricle it can worsen decompensation. Beta blockers are first-line rate control for AF without heart failure.
key_concept:
AF rate control: pick the drug by the comorbidity.
  • AF alone: beta blocker
  • AF + asthma/COPD or claudication: diltiazem/verapamil
  • AF + heart failure (low EF): digoxin; in stable HFrEF an HF-proven beta blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol) is also first line, not propranolol
  • Avoid diltiazem/verapamil when EF is low
  • Unstable AF: electrical cardioversion
exam_pearl: Ivabradine is a trap: it lowers sinus rate only, so it is useless once the rhythm is AF.

stem: Elderly Patient Presents With Acute Heart Failure And Has Atrial Fibrillation On ECG. What Is The Best Next Step?
why_right: "Acute heart failure" with AF on ECG in an elderly patient: the safe rate-control drug is digoxin, because it slows the ventricular response without reducing contractility. In acutely decompensated failure, negatively inotropic agents can precipitate cardiogenic shock, so digoxin is preferred here.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenosine: terminates re-entrant SVT by transient AV block; in AF it only briefly slows the rate and gives no sustained control. Right answer for stable narrow-complex regular SVT.
C. Beta blocker: first-line rate control for AF without heart failure, but starting it during acute decompensation can worsen failure; it is introduced once the patient is stable (HFrEF chronic therapy).
D. Procainamide: a class Ia antiarrhythmic used for pre-excited AF (WPW) or some wide-complex tachycardias; it is negatively inotropic and has no role in rate control here.
key_concept:
AF + acute heart failure = digoxin for rate control.
  • Unstable (shock, hypotension): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable AF + HF: digoxin
  • Stable AF, normal LV: beta blocker or diltiazem
  • AF + WPW: procainamide, avoid AV nodal blockers
  • Adenosine is for SVT, not AF
exam_pearl: "Acute" heart failure is the clue that rules out the beta blocker that would otherwise be first line.

stem: Patient with acute kidney injury, how to know if the cause is cholesterol emboli?
why_right: The lead-in asks how to tell the AKI is due to "cholesterol emboli". Eosinophiluria is the urinary hallmark of atheroembolic renal disease, typically after arterial catheterization or vascular surgery, often with livedo reticularis, blue toes, peripheral eosinophilia and low complement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Red cell casts: indicate glomerular bleeding, i.e. glomerulonephritis or vasculitis (nephritic picture).
B. Epithelial casts: renal tubular epithelial cells and muddy brown granular casts point to acute tubular necrosis (ischemic or nephrotoxic).
C. Hyaline casts: nonspecific; seen in concentrated urine, prerenal azotemia or even normal people.
key_concept:
Urine sediment points to the site of injury.
  • RBC casts: glomerulonephritis
  • WBC casts: pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis
  • Muddy brown granular / epithelial casts: ATN
  • Hyaline casts: prerenal or normal
  • Eosinophiluria: cholesterol emboli (also AIN)
exam_pearl: Eosinophiluria + recent catheterization = cholesterol emboli; eosinophiluria + new drug with fever and rash = AIN.

stem: A 55-year-old man with acute coronary syndrome who recently underwent cardiac catheterization is evaluated because of acute kidney injury. Which of the following is most suggestive of cholesterol emboli as a cause of acute renal failure?
why_right: AKI after cardiac catheterization points to atheroembolic (cholesterol emboli) renal disease, where catheter manipulation dislodges plaque into small renal arteries. The urinary hallmark is eosinophiluria, often with blood eosinophilia, low complement, livedo reticularis and blue toes.
why_wrong_block:
A. WBC casts point to pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis, not embolic disease.
B. RBC casts point to glomerulonephritis or vasculitis.
C. Granular (muddy brown) casts point to acute tubular necrosis, e.g. contrast nephropathy after catheterization; they do not suggest emboli.
key_concept:
Urine sediment decoder:
  • RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs: glomerulonephritis, vasculitis
  • WBC casts: pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis
  • Muddy brown granular casts: ATN
  • Eosinophiluria: cholesterol emboli (also AIN)
exam_pearl: Post catheter AKI has two answers: contrast ATN (granular casts) vs cholesterol emboli (eosinophiluria); read which cause the question names.

stem: Patient with severe mitral valve STENOSIS due to RF and a fib, what is used for secondary stroke prevention?
why_right: "Severe mitral valve STENOSIS" due to rheumatic fever with AF is so-called valvular AF, which carries a very high thromboembolic risk. Warfarin (target INR 2 to 3) is the anticoagulant of choice; DOACs are not recommended in moderate to severe mitral stenosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin: antiplatelet therapy does not adequately prevent cardioembolic stroke in AF; it is used for atherothrombotic (non-cardioembolic) stroke prevention.
C. Apixaban: a DOAC suited to non-valvular AF, including AF with mitral regurgitation; it is not recommended in moderate to severe mitral stenosis or with mechanical valves, where warfarin is used.
key_concept:
Anticoagulant choice in AF depends on the valve.
  • Moderate to severe mitral stenosis: warfarin
  • Mechanical valve: warfarin
  • Mitral regurgitation, other native valve disease: DOAC acceptable
  • Warfarin target INR in AF: 2 to 3
  • Aspirin is not stroke prevention for AF
exam_pearl: STENOSIS (rheumatic MS) = warfarin; regurgitation = DOAC is fine.

stem: Patient with severe mitral valve REGURGITATION due to RF and a fib, what is used for secondary stroke prevention?
why_right: The key word is "REGURGITATION": AF with mitral regurgitation is treated as non-valvular AF, because only moderate to severe mitral stenosis and mechanical valves are excluded from DOAC use. So a DOAC such as apixaban is appropriate and preferred over warfarin for stroke prevention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin: antiplatelet therapy is not adequate stroke prevention in AF; it is for atherothrombotic disease.
B. Warfarin: effective, but needed specifically for moderate to severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valves; with MR a DOAC is preferred (fewer bleeds, no INR monitoring). The source flagged warfarin with a question mark, but apixaban is its key.
key_concept:
"Valvular AF" (warfarin only) means moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve.
  • AF + severe MS: warfarin
  • AF + severe MR: apixaban or any DOAC
  • AF alone: beta blocker for rate
  • AF + claudication: diltiazem for rate
  • AF + heart failure: digoxin for rate
exam_pearl: The paired recall swaps one word: STENOSIS = warfarin, REGURGITATION = apixaban.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: C marked ✅✅; B also highlighted but followed by a question mark. stem: An elderly patient receiving IV heparin develops deep vein thrombosis 6 days post-operatively. Platelet count is 75 ×109/L. What is the best next step in management?
why_right: New thrombosis ("deep vein thrombosis 6 days" into IV heparin) with a platelet fall to 75 fits heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (type II), an antibody against the PF4-heparin complex that is prothrombotic. Management is to stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant; argatroban, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is the classic first-line choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start warfarin: not started during acute HIT because early protein C depletion can cause venous limb gangrene; it is begun only after platelets recover, overlapping with a non-heparin agent.
B. Start enoxaparin: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies and is contraindicated; it is the right first-line agent for ordinary DVT without HIT.
C. Transfuse platelets: HIT causes clotting, not bleeding, and transfusion may fuel thrombosis; reserved for active serious bleeding.
key_concept:
HIT = platelet drop of about 50% (or new thrombosis) 5 to 10 days after heparin.
  • Step 1: stop ALL heparin, including LMWH and flushes
  • Step 2: non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or DOAC in selected cases
  • Warfarin only after platelet recovery
  • Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion
exam_pearl: Low platelets plus a NEW clot on heparin means HIT, which is prothrombotic: switch the anticoagulant, do not stop anticoagulating.
compiler_note: Compiler note: HIT type II: thrombocytopenia + thrombosis 5-10 days after heparin = stop heparin + start argatroban ✅. Immune-mediated (antibodies against heparin-PF4 complex) causing platelet activation and paradoxical thrombosis; prothrombotic, not bleeding. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor, first line for HIT (UpToDate). ASH 2018 HIT guidelines: stop all heparin, start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban ✅, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOACs in selected cases). Do NOT start warfarin until platelets recover (>150). Alternate recalls: Q: male after hip operation, DVT day 6 on IV heparin, low platelets: A Warfarin B Aspirin C Enoxaparin D Argatroban (highlighted). Screenshot (next page): lower limb or hip operation, DVT day 6 on IV heparin, platelets 90 (150-400), additional medication: same options, Answer: D.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents for a routine follow-up. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or hypertension. His physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory investigations reveal: LDL cholesterol: within normal range HDL cholesterol: borderline low Triglycerides: significantly elevated (300) What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: The patient is already on "maximum dose statin" with normal LDL, and the residual problem is moderately raised triglycerides (300). This recall keys omega-3 fatty acids as the add-on to lower triglycerides: they lower TG without the myopathy concern of a statin-fibrate combination, and high-dose purified omega-3 (icosapent ethyl) is the TG agent with outcome data on top of a statin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Statin: he is already at maximum dose and LDL is at goal; statins mainly lower LDL, so more statin cannot address the triglycerides.
C. Niacin: raises HDL and lowers triglycerides, but adding it to statins showed no cardiovascular benefit and causes flushing, hyperglycemia and hepatotoxicity; largely abandoned.
D. Fibrate: the drug of choice when triglycerides are very high (≥500 mg/dL) to prevent pancreatitis; at moderate levels on top of a statin it adds myopathy risk without proven outcome benefit.
key_concept:
Residual hypertriglyceridemia on statin: match the agent to the TG level.
  • Raised LDL: statin, then ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitor
  • Moderate TG on max statin: omega-3 fatty acids (this recall's key)
  • Very high TG (≥500 mg/dL): fibrate to prevent pancreatitis
  • Always: lifestyle, alcohol reduction, secondary causes (diabetes, hypothyroidism)
exam_pearl: Pancreatitis-range triglycerides flip the answer to fibrate.

stem: patients with hx of heart disease present with SOB and pink frothy spetum ?
why_right: "History of heart disease" with SOB and "pink frothy sputum" is acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema from left heart failure. The failing pump lowers cardiac output, and the body compensates with sympathetic vasoconstriction, so systemic vascular resistance is HIGH (cold, clammy peripheries), with a raised PCWP.
why_wrong_block:
A. High CO: cardiac output is low in pump failure; high CO with low SVR is the profile of septic (distributive) shock.
C. Low PCWP: pulmonary edema from LV failure means a HIGH wedge pressure; low PCWP fits hypovolemic, septic or neurogenic states (or non-cardiogenic ARDS with normal PCWP).
D. Low something: this option was not fully recalled. Note that if it read "low cardiac output" it would also be true in cardiogenic failure; the source key for this recall is high SVR.
key_concept:
Hemodynamic profiles (CO / PCWP / SVR):
  • Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP high, SVR high
  • Hypovolemic: CO low, PCWP low, SVR high
  • Septic: CO high, PCWP low, SVR low
  • Neurogenic: CO low, HR low, SVR low
  • Only cardiogenic has a high PCWP
exam_pearl: Pink frothy sputum = left heart failure: high PCWP and high SVR; a high CO points to sepsis instead.

stem: An elderly patient presents with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and signs of heart failure. Echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with a normal ejection fraction (60%). What is the most likely diagnosis?
OptC: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
why_right: An elderly patient with heart failure symptoms ("exertional dyspnea, orthopnea") and echo showing "concentric left ventricular hypertrophy" with a "normal ejection fraction (60%)" has heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The stiff, hypertrophied ventricle fills poorly (diastolic dysfunction), usually from long-standing hypertension, while systolic function is maintained.
why_wrong_block:
A. Restrictive cardiomyopathy: also preserved EF, but from infiltration (e.g. amyloid) with non-dilated stiff ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and often low-voltage ECG, not a simple concentric hypertensive LVH picture.
B. Constrictive pericarditis: thickened/calcified pericardium with Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock and right-sided congestion predominating; the myocardium itself is not hypertrophied. Think after TB, radiation or cardiac surgery.
key_concept:
Heart failure classified by EF.
  • HFrEF: EF ≤40%, dilated ventricle
  • HFpEF: EF ≥50%, often concentric LVH, elderly hypertensive
  • Clue: S4 = stiff noncompliant ventricle
  • Poorly controlled HTN → LVH → diastolic dysfunction
exam_pearl: HF symptoms with a normal EF and concentric LVH = HFpEF; biatrial enlargement with low voltage suggests restrictive instead.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus who was maintained on mycophenolate mofetil 1 gm/day, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/day, and prednisone 5 mg/day for the last 1 year. She has had inactive disease for more than 6 months. She is planning to get pregnant (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate action at this time?
OptC: Discontinue mycophenolate mofetil and start azathioprine
OptD: Discontinue mycophenolate mofetil and start methotrexate
why_right: She has had inactive SLE for more than 6 months (the right time to plan conception) and is planning pregnancy. Mycophenolate mofetil is teratogenic and must be stopped before conception, and azathioprine is the pregnancy-compatible replacement to keep the disease quiet. Hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisone are both compatible with pregnancy and are continued.
why_wrong_block:
A. Discontinue prednisone and start cyclosporine: prednisone 5 mg is compatible with pregnancy and is not the problem; this leaves the teratogenic MMF in place.
B. Discontinue hydroxychloroquine and start quinacrine: hydroxychloroquine is safe in pregnancy and should be continued (stopping it raises flare risk); MMF is still left on.
D. Discontinue mycophenolate mofetil and start methotrexate: right drug stopped, but methotrexate is also teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy.
key_concept:
SLE pregnancy planning: quiet disease for about 6 months, then swap teratogens for safe drugs.
  • Continue: hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine, low to moderate dose prednisone, low-dose aspirin
  • Stop before conception: mycophenolate, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, leflunomide
  • MMF is replaced by azathioprine
exam_pearl: Two options stop MMF: pick the replacement that is itself safe in pregnancy (azathioprine, not methotrexate).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem mentions lab results that are not shown on the page.

stem: A Patient presented with weight loss, diarrhea that sometimes with blood. Colonoscopy: Linear ulcer, stricture, segmental involvement normal and inflamed mucosa What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Colonoscopy shows "linear ulcer, stricture, segmental involvement" with normal mucosa between inflamed areas: skip lesions, deep linear (fissuring) ulcers and strictures are hallmarks of transmural Crohn's disease. Weight loss and diarrhea, sometimes bloody, fit as well.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ulcerative colitis: mucosal disease that starts in the rectum and extends continuously proximally, with no skip areas and rare strictures; think UC with bloody diarrhea, urgency and continuous colitis.
C. Irritable bowel syndrome: a functional disorder with a normal colonoscopy and no weight loss or blood; alarm features exclude it.
key_concept:
Crohn's vs UC on endoscopy.
  • Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, linear ulcers, cobblestoning, strictures, fistulas, granulomas
  • UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal only, pseudopolyps, no fistulas
  • Crohn's: often RLQ (terminal ileum); UC: LLQ, bloody diarrhea
exam_pearl: Skip lesions or strictures mean Crohn's even if the diarrhea is bloody.

stem: After Blood Transfusion For 15 Minutes Patient Becomes Hypotensive With SpO₂ 88% — Diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive pair is hypotension plus hypoxemia (SpO₂ 88%) developing during the transfusion. That respiratory picture is the signature of transfusion related acute lung injury (TRALI): donor antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the lung, causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, low saturations and low blood pressure within the first hours of transfusion. Nothing in the stem points to hemolysis (no fever, flank or infusion site pain, dark urine) or to allergy (no urticaria, itch, wheeze).
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: also starts within minutes and can drop the BP, but it is led by fever, chills, infusion site or flank/back pain, chest tightness and hemoglobinuria (usually ABO error); hypoxemia is not its hallmark.
C. Allergic reaction: the simple form is urticaria and itch with stable vitals; it would be right if the stem described a rash. Anaphylaxis would add wheeze, stridor or angioedema, none of which are given here.
key_concept:
Transfusion reaction with HYPOXIA = think lung: TRALI vs TACO.
  • TRALI: hypoxemia + hypotension, fever possible, noncardiogenic edema, within hours
  • TACO: hypoxemia + hypertension, raised JVP, volume overload (elderly, cardiac/renal)
  • Acute hemolytic: fever, flank/infusion site pain, hemoglobinuria, DIC; ABO error
  • Febrile nonhemolytic: fever and chills only, vitals otherwise stable
  • Allergic: urticaria/itch; anaphylaxis: wheeze, angioedema, shock (IgA deficiency)
  • Any reaction: stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with saline
exam_pearl: Hypoxia with LOW BP = TRALI; hypoxia with HIGH BP and raised JVP = TACO; fever with flank pain = hemolysis.

stem: Elderly man DM HTN was admitted to the ward due to acute abdomen, during laparotomy surgical team found necrotic bowel and wanted to exclude cardiac causes, his ECG showed sinus rhythm, Echo was normal. What should you do next?
why_right: Necrotic bowel in an elderly diabetic hypertensive raises acute mesenteric ischemia, and the commonest cardiac source is embolism from atrial fibrillation. A single ECG in sinus rhythm and a normal echo (no thrombus, no valve disease) do not exclude paroxysmal AF. Ambulatory Holter monitoring (24 to 48 hours or longer) is the next step to capture intermittent AF that could embolise.
why_wrong_block:
A. Exercise ECG looks for inducible ischemia in suspected stable angina; coronary disease does not cause mesenteric emboli, so it does not answer the cardiac embolic question.
C. The echo is already normal; repeating it adds nothing. If a hidden source were still suspected, transoesophageal echo (not a repeat transthoracic study) would be the step after rhythm monitoring.
D. This option was not recalled in the source, so it cannot be assessed; the decision point is excluding paroxysmal AF.
key_concept:
Embolic event (mesenteric ischemia or stroke) + normal ECG and echo: look for paroxysmal AF.
  • Holter (24 to 48 h): intermittent AF or frequent paroxysmal arrhythmia
  • Infrequent episodes: event recorder or implantable loop recorder
  • Echo (TTE then TEE): thrombus, valve disease, PFO
  • Exercise ECG: stable angina workup, not embolic source
exam_pearl: Sinus rhythm on one ECG never excludes AF; the next step is prolonged rhythm monitoring.

stem: When to resume chemotherapy after tumor lysis syndrome?
why_right: This recall's key is uric acid <475.83, creatinine <141, urine pH >7. The uric acid figure is the SI conversion of 8 mg/dL, the laboratory threshold used to define tumor lysis syndrome (Cairo-Bishop), so falling below it means the urate load has been cleared. A creatinine <141 µmol/L (about 1.6 mg/dL) indicates recovery of renal function, and the pH value is the source's alkaline urine target. Only option B combines all three of the source's cut-offs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uric acid <356 (about 6 mg/dL) is a stricter target than the TLS defining threshold that this recall uses; the creatinine and pH are the same as B, so the uric acid value is the error.
C. Creatinine <229 µmol/L still reflects significant ongoing acute kidney injury; resuming nephrotoxic, lysis inducing chemotherapy on an unrecovered kidney risks recurrent TLS.
D. Urine pH >8 is over alkalinization; very alkaline urine promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in the tubules, worsening renal injury.
key_concept:
TLS = cell contents flood the blood and injure the kidney; restart therapy only after labs and renal function recover.
  • Lab pattern: high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, LOW calcium
  • Uric acid 8 mg/dL ≈ 476 µmol/L (the TLS laboratory threshold)
  • Prevention: aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol (blocks xanthine oxidase)
  • Established or high risk: rasburicase (converts uric acid to allantoin)
  • Hyperkalemia is the lethal early problem (arrhythmia)
  • Calcium phosphate deposition and urate crystals cause the AKI
exam_pearl: Memorize 475.83 as 8 mg/dL uric acid; the wrong options each change exactly one number (uric acid too strict, creatinine too high, pH too alkaline).

stem: patient came with pneumonia sx productive cough, fever, pain, pic was provided (lobar pneumonia), treatment was initiated (IV cetriaxone, paracetamol, tramadol), after one day he became stable and improved what drug to stop? Reduced platelets count (around 70 I think)
why_right: The new problem is thrombocytopenia (platelets about 70) appearing after treatment was started, in a patient whose pneumonia is otherwise improving. Among the drugs actually given, ceftriaxone is the recognized cause of drug induced immune thrombocytopenia (drug dependent antibodies destroy platelets), so it is the drug to stop. Because he is now stable, the antibiotic can be switched to an appropriate non beta lactam or oral alternative to complete the course.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paracetamol: thrombocytopenia is extremely rare; it is a safe antipyretic and analgesic and would only be stopped for hepatotoxicity concerns.
B. Tramadol: its adverse effects are mainly CNS (sedation, seizures, serotonin syndrome) and nausea, not platelet destruction.
D. Vancomycin: it can cause immune thrombocytopenia, but it was never given to this patient, so it cannot be the culprit.
key_concept:
New cytopenia after starting drugs: identify the most likely culprit among drugs ACTUALLY given and stop it.
  • Drug induced immune thrombocytopenia: platelets fall typically 1 to 2 weeks after first exposure, sooner on re-exposure
  • Common culprits: beta lactams (cephalosporins, penicillins), vancomycin, heparin, quinine, sulfonamides, valproate
  • Management: stop the drug; platelets usually recover within days
  • On heparin: think HIT (4T score) instead
exam_pearl: Read the option list against the drugs given: vancomycin is a real cause but a trap here because it was never started.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0267).
Compiler note: Key new finding is thrombocytopenia (~70,000) after starting treatment. Paracetamol: thrombocytopenia extremely rare. Tramadol: mainly CNS side effects. Ceftriaxone ✅ known cause of immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. Vancomycin: can cause it but was not given. Cephalosporins cause drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (antibodies destroy platelets). Management: stop the offending drug immediately and switch to another appropriate antibiotic if needed.

stem: A 78-year-old man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease is complaining of fatigue and nausea. He denies any change in consciousness, seizures, abdominal pain, vomiting, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He is on insulin, lisinopril, amlodipine, erythropoietin, and vitamin D. Examination reveals that he is drowsy but not in distress (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? Hidden GB Labs Are: K: 6.2 (Or 6.3), Na: 141
why_right: An elderly man with CKD, diabetes and on lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) has K 6.2 to 6.3 with fatigue, nausea and drowsiness. Significant symptomatic hyperkalemia is an emergency, and the first step is to stabilize the cardiac membrane with IV calcium gluconate, which acts within minutes to prevent arrhythmia even though it does not lower potassium. Shifting and removal follow after the heart is protected.
why_wrong_block:
A. NaHCO3: shifts potassium into cells and is reserved for patients with metabolic acidosis, given after calcium; it does not protect the myocardium.
B. D5 water: dextrose alone does not treat hyperkalemia; glucose is given together with insulin as the shifting step (and to prevent hypoglycemia), after calcium.
C. Diuretics: loop diuretics remove potassium (step 3) and work slowly, especially in CKD; they come after stabilization and shifting.
key_concept:
Hyperkalemia ladder: PROTECT, SHIFT, REMOVE, PREVENT.
  • 1. Protect: IV calcium gluconate (no effect on K level)
  • 2. Shift: insulin + glucose, salbutamol, bicarbonate only if acidotic
  • 3. Remove: loop diuretics, binders (kayexalate), dialysis if severe or refractory
  • 4. Prevent: stop ACE inhibitor/ARB, spironolactone
  • ECG: peaked T waves, then wide QRS
exam_pearl: If calcium gluconate is among the options in a significant or symptomatic hyperkalemia stem, it is the first step; when it is missing, move down the ladder.
compiler_note: Compiler note: If K >= 6 or symptoms/ECG concern = Calcium gluconate FIRST, always. CKD, K 6.2-6.3, fatigue + drowsiness (possible cardiac conduction effect). Hyperkalemia >= 6.0 or symptomatic = emergency; stabilize cardiac membrane with calcium gluconate (acts within minutes, protects myocardium, does NOT lower K but prevents arrhythmia). Order: 1) protect heart: IV calcium gluconate; 2) shift K into cells: insulin + glucose, beta-agonist, +/- bicarbonate; 3) remove K: diuretics, binders, dialysis. Refs: KDIGO, Harrison's.

stem: A 78-year-old man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease is complaining of fatigue and nausea. He denies any change in consciousness, seizures, abdominal pain, vomiting, chest pain, or shortness of breath. He is on insulin, lisinopril, amlodipine, erythropoietin, and vitamin D. Examination reveals that he is drowsy but not in distress (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? Hidden GB Labs Are: K: 6.2 (Or 6.3), Na: 141
why_right: Same patient as the calcium gluconate version, but calcium is not offered. This recall's key is dialysis because the CKD here looks advanced (he is on erythropoietin and vitamin D), so the kidneys cannot excrete potassium and diuretics will be ineffective; dialysis is the definitive way to remove potassium. The remaining options are either conditional (bicarbonate only if acidotic) or do not treat hyperkalemia at all (dextrose water alone).
why_wrong_block:
A. NaHCO3: a temporary shifting agent useful only when metabolic acidosis is present; it does not remove potassium and its effect in this setting is modest.
B. D5 water: dextrose without insulin does not lower potassium meaningfully; glucose is only used with insulin as a shifting step.
C. Diuretics: they rely on renal excretion, which is poor in advanced CKD; they are right for hyperkalemia with preserved renal function or fluid overload.
key_concept:
When the first rung (calcium) is missing, pick the next best rung that fits the patient.
  • Protect: calcium gluconate
  • Shift: insulin + glucose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic
  • Remove: diuretics (need working kidneys), binders, dialysis
  • Dialysis: severe or refractory hyperkalemia, or advanced CKD/ESRD where excretion fails
  • Clues to advanced CKD: erythropoietin, vitamin D analogue use
exam_pearl: Calcium gluconate present = choose it; calcium absent in advanced CKD = dialysis is the definitive removal.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In CKD patients, significant hyperkalemia often cannot be corrected effectively by renal excretion. Definitive treatment = Dialysis. (Same stem as 132 but calcium gluconate not among options.)

stem: A patient with interstitial lung disease presents with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), a loud pulmonary component of S2, prominent V waves, and pulsatile hepatomegaly. What is the most likely cause?
why_right: Interstitial lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension (loud P2), which overloads the right ventricle and leads to cor pulmonale with functional tricuspid regurgitation. The specific TR signs are the prominent v waves in the JVP and pulsatile hepatomegaly, as the regurgitant jet transmits back into the neck veins and liver. TR gives a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that increases with inspiration.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aortic regurgitation: a left sided lesion with an early diastolic murmur, collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure; it causes left heart failure, not giant v waves or a pulsatile liver.
C. Mitral regurgitation: causes left sided failure (PND, pulmonary edema) with an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; the PND here is a distractor, and MR does not give v waves in the JVP or a pulsatile liver.
D. Pulmonary regurgitation: can accompany pulmonary hypertension (Graham Steell early diastolic murmur), but it does not explain prominent v waves and pulsatile hepatomegaly, which are specific to TR.
key_concept:
Lung disease → pulmonary hypertension → RV strain → functional TR.
  • Prominent (giant) v wave in JVP = TR
  • Pulsatile hepatomegaly = TR
  • Loud P2 = pulmonary hypertension; parasternal heave = RVH
  • TR murmur: pansystolic, left lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration
  • Cannon a waves = complete heart block; absent a waves = AF
exam_pearl: Do not let PND pull you to the left heart: v waves plus a pulsatile liver lock the answer to tricuspid regurgitation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): 55-year-old woman with ILD, exertional dyspnea and bilateral LL edema; elevated JVP with prominent v wave, pulsating hepatomegaly, left parasternal heave, loud P2. Most expected additional finding on auscultation? A. Mitral regurgitation B. Aortic regurgitation C. Tricuspid regurgitation D. Pulmonary regurgitation (highlighted: C. Tricuspid regurgitation).

stem: A 32-year-old man came to the clinic for follow-up visit. He is diagnosed of ileocolonic Crohn's disease started on steroid and pentasa for 3 months. He noticed perineal pain and discharges for 3 weeks duration. His abdominal symptoms are well controlled with no abdominal pain or diarrhea. Examination was normal apart from 2 perianal fistula were seen RBC 4 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) Hb 11 130-170 g/L (Male) Platelets count 421 150-400 x 109/L WBC 7 4.5-10.5 x 109/L ESR 36 2-10 mm/h (Male) MRI Pelvis: Confirmed the presence of perianal fistulae. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
why_right: Luminal Crohn's is controlled, but he now has two perianal fistulae confirmed on MRI pelvis. Fistulizing Crohn's disease is an indication for anti-TNF biologic therapy, and infliximab is the agent with the strongest evidence for fistula closure and maintenance. The other options do not heal fistulae on their own.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate: an immunomodulator for steroid dependent luminal Crohn's (or alongside a biologic); it is not the treatment of choice for perianal fistulae.
B. Azathioprine: slow acting maintenance immunomodulator; alone it is insufficient for fistulizing disease and is mainly used in combination with infliximab.
C. Budesonide: an ileal release steroid for inducing remission in mild to moderate ileocecal luminal disease; steroids do not heal fistulae and are not for maintenance.
key_concept:
Crohn's ladder: steroids induce, immunomodulators maintain, biologics for refractory or FISTULIZING disease.
  • Induction: budesonide (ileal) or IV methylprednisolone (severe)
  • Maintenance: azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate
  • Fistulizing or refractory: infliximab or adalimumab (often with azathioprine)
  • Perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis to map; drain any abscess (seton) before biologics
  • Screen for TB and hepatitis B before anti-TNF
exam_pearl: Perianal fistula in Crohn's = anti-TNF (infliximab); if the stem adds fever and fluctuance, the next step is imaging and drainage first.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with Sjogren's syndrome on hydroxychloroquine is evaluated in the clinic because of fatigue. Her physical examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following renal tubular acidosis type is the most likely cause of her hypokalemia?
why_right: Sjogren's syndrome is a classic autoimmune cause of distal (type 1) RTA, where impaired distal H+ secretion gives a non anion gap acidosis with hypokalemia and urine pH above 5.5. Her fatigue fits muscle weakness from low potassium.
why_wrong_block:
B. Proximal (type 2) RTA also has low potassium but is caused by Fanconi syndrome, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or multiple myeloma, not Sjogren's.
C. Type 3 is a rare mixed proximal and distal form (carbonic anhydrase II deficiency), not linked to Sjogren's.
D. Type 4 RTA is from aldosterone deficiency or resistance and causes hyperkalemia, the opposite of this patient.
key_concept:
All RTAs: non anion gap, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
  • Type 1 (distal): low K, urine pH > 5.5, stones; Sjogren's, SLE, amphotericin B
  • Type 2 (proximal): low K, milder acidosis; Fanconi, acetazolamide, myeloma
  • Type 4: high K, urine pH < 5.5; diabetes, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, adrenal insufficiency
  • Treat type 1 with bicarbonate or potassium citrate
exam_pearl: Potassium splits them: high K = type 4; low K + Sjogren's/SLE = type 1.

stem: A 35y old man complaining of sore throat, fatigue, body aches, and cough with white sputum. After it's associated with streaks of blood. Examination of cardio and chest normal. Chest X-Ray : normal. What's the diagnosis?
why_right: A young healthy man with an upper respiratory prodrome (sore throat, fatigue, body aches) develops a productive cough with white sputum that later shows blood streaks, with a normal chest exam and normal chest X-ray. That is acute bronchitis, usually viral and one of the most common causes of minor hemoptysis. The normal CXR rules out pneumonia and pulmonary edema.
why_wrong_block:
B. Pulmonary edema: presents with dyspnea, orthopnea, basal crackles and an abnormal CXR (congestion, effusions); this chest exam and film are normal.
C. Goodpasture syndrome: anti GBM disease combining pulmonary hemorrhage with glomerulonephritis (hematuria, rising creatinine); no renal features here.
D. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia: recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias and family history, sometimes AVMs; not an acute URTI picture.
key_concept:
Blood streaked sputum: match the companion clue.
  • URTI prodrome + normal CXR = acute bronchitis
  • Fever + consolidation on CXR = pneumonia
  • Hemoptysis + hematuria/high creatinine = Goodpasture (or GPA)
  • Epistaxis + telangiectasias = HHT
  • Dyspnea + basal crackles = pulmonary edema
  • Smoker with weight loss or persistent hemoptysis = investigate for cancer
exam_pearl: Blood streaks do not make it serious: URTI symptoms plus a normal chest X-ray in a young patient = acute bronchitis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): A 36-year-old previously healthy man in primary healthcare with cough, fatigue, sore throat and body aches; productive whitish sputum with occasional blood streaks; chest exam normal; CXR normal without consolidation. Same options. Answer: A.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with 9-months history of worsening dysphagia for both solid and liquid. Recently she had episodes of ill defined central chest discomfort and nocturnal cough. Clinical examination was unremarkable (see lab results). RBC 5 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 11.8 130-170 g/L. (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 300 150-400 x 109/L WBC 7 4.5-10.5 x 109/L ESR 13 2-10 mm/h (Male), 3-15 mm/h (Female). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: dysphagia for both solid and liquid
why_right: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset points to a motility disorder, not a mechanical obstruction. Achalasia (failure of LES relaxation with absent peristalsis) also explains the ill defined central chest discomfort and nocturnal cough from retained food being regurgitated and aspirated at night. A 9 month course in a 45 year old with near normal labs fits achalasia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Esophageal web: intermittent dysphagia mainly to solids, classically with iron deficiency anemia in middle aged women (Plummer-Vinson); it does not explain dysphagia to liquids or nocturnal cough.
C. Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker): elderly patient with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, a neck swelling or gurgle; it is a high (oropharyngeal) problem.
D. Squamous cancer of esophagus: progressive dysphagia to solids first, then liquids, with marked weight loss in an older patient (smoking, alcohol); not liquid dysphagia from the start.
key_concept:
Solids AND liquids from the start = motility; solids then liquids = mechanical.
  • Achalasia: both, regurgitation, nocturnal cough, chest pain; barium bird's beak; manometry confirms
  • Cancer: progressive solids to liquids, weight loss, older
  • Web: solids, iron deficiency anemia
  • Zenker: elderly, halitosis, regurgitation of old food, neck gurgle
  • Workup: endoscopy first to exclude cancer (pseudoachalasia), then manometry
exam_pearl: Liquids as hard to swallow as solids from day one = achalasia; liquids only late in the story = cancer.

stem: A 40-year-old man is admitted with palpitations of 4-hour duration. He had similar attack a month ago but did not seek medical advice. His initial electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. He subsequently converted to sinus rhythm. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate to maintain sinus rhythm?
why_right: The lead in is maintain sinus rhythm after a recurrent AF episode has converted, which is rhythm control. Amiodarone is the only antiarrhythmic in the list that prevents AF recurrence; the other three only slow the ventricular rate. So among these options amiodarone is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Digoxin: a rate control drug (preferred when AF coexists with heart failure or in sedentary patients); it does not maintain sinus rhythm.
B. Bisoprolol: a beta blocker used first line for rate control in stable AF; it would be right if the question asked to control the ventricular rate.
C. Verapamil: a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for rate control; avoid in heart failure with reduced EF, and it does not keep the patient in sinus rhythm.
key_concept:
Read the verb: control RATE vs maintain RHYTHM.
  • Rate control: beta blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin (AF + HF)
  • Rhythm control: amiodarone (works with structural heart disease)
  • No structural disease: class IC (flecainide) is often preferred in practice
  • Unstable AF: immediate electrical cardioversion
  • Anticoagulation decided separately by CHA2DS2-VA score
exam_pearl: "Maintain sinus rhythm" = rhythm control drug; digoxin, bisoprolol and verapamil only slow the rate.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Marked 'MG' (MedGard endorsement).

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents to the Outpatient Department. She has been unwell for 6 months with arthralgia, fever, weight loss, and more recently has developed pleuritic chest pains. She also has synovitis of the small joints of the hands. There were no rashes or nail fold infarcts. Heart sounds are normal (see lab results and reports). BP 110/70, HR 70, RR 18. Hb 89 (120-160 g/L), WBC 3.2 (4-10.5), Platelet count 99 (150-400), Neutrophils 80%, Lymphocytes 17%, MCV 90, CRP 99 (<8.2 mg/L), ESR 56 (3-15), Clotting time 7, Ferritin 920 (22-340), ANA 1:320 (=1:40). Pulmonary Angiography CT: Confirms a small left pleural effusion. There is no consolidation, pulmonary embolism, and no lymphadenopathy. ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: synovitis of the small joints of the hands
why_right: A middle-aged woman with 6 months of fever, weight loss and arthralgia, small-joint synovitis, serositis (pleuritic pain with a small pleural effusion) and a high-titre ANA 1:320 fits SLE. The pancytopenia (Hb 89, WBC 3.2, platelets 99) is a classic lupus feature from immune destruction and is the clue that separates SLE from other inflammatory arthritides. CTPA excluded PE and pneumonia, leaving lupus serositis as the cause of the pleuritic pain.
why_wrong_block:
A. Infective endocarditis causes fever and arthralgia, but expect a new murmur, embolic phenomena and leukocytosis; heart sounds are normal and there are no nail fold infarcts here.
B. Adult-onset Still's disease gives fever, arthritis and very high ferritin, but with neutrophilic leukocytosis, a salmon rash and a negative ANA; this patient is leukopenic with a high-titre ANA.
D. Rheumatoid vasculitis occurs in long-standing seropositive, nodular RA and causes skin ulcers or nail fold infarcts; no RA history, no nodules and no infarcts here, and RA does not explain pancytopenia with serositis.
key_concept:
Multisystem disease in a woman + cytopenias + serositis + arthritis + positive ANA = SLE.
  • SLE: leukopenia/lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia
  • Still's: leukocytosis, ferritin very high, ANA and RF negative, evanescent salmon rash
  • Endocarditis: murmur, emboli, positive blood cultures
  • Rheumatoid vasculitis: long-standing seropositive RA, nail fold infarcts, ulcers
  • Confirm SLE with anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith and low C3/C4
exam_pearl: High ferritin tempts Still's, but Still's has a high WBC and negative ANA; leukopenia plus high-titre ANA keeps it lupus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Full recall (#rheumatology) with labs given on next page; C marked ✅MG. Typed short version also highlights C.

stem: A 60-year-old man known to have hypertension and post aortic valve replacement on lisinopril 20 mg, amlodipine 5 mg and warfarin 3 mg once daily. He was admitted to the hospital with history of productive cough and shortness of breath, and was found to have positive acid fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum. First line four anti-TB drugs were started. Which of the following regarding medications should be done?
OptA: Lisinopril dose needs to be decreased
