why_right: The first-line four anti-TB drugs include rifampicin, a potent hepatic enzyme (CYP450) inducer that speeds warfarin metabolism and lowers its effect. In a patient with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin, a falling INR risks valve thrombosis, so warfarin must be increased with close INR monitoring. When rifampicin is later stopped, the warfarin dose must be reduced again.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lisinopril has no clinically important interaction with first-line anti-TB drugs, so no dose reduction is needed.
B. Rifampicin can lower amlodipine levels, but that would call for monitoring BP or adjusting the dose, not stopping the drug; it is not the critical interaction here.
D. Rifampicin is a core drug of the first-line regimen for confirmed AFB-positive TB; the correct response to an interaction is to adjust the interacting drug, not drop the TB backbone.
key_concept:
Rifampicin = enzyme inducer: it lowers levels of drugs metabolised by the liver.
  • Warfarin: increase dose, check INR closely
  • Oral contraceptives: become unreliable, use another method
  • Steroids, some antiretrovirals and azoles: levels fall
  • When rifampicin stops: reduce warfarin back
  • Isoniazid is the opposite (enzyme inhibitor, e.g. raises phenytoin)
exam_pearl: If the stem asks what happens when rifampicin is STOPPED, the answer flips to reducing warfarin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Repeated as Q: with same options (C highlighted), and another version: 'Which of the following medications needs to be adjusted? A. Lisinopril B. Amlodipine C. Warfarin D. Rifampin' (C. Warfarin highlighted).

stem: A 40-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department for several episodes of hematemesis. He has no previous similar episodes. His history is unremarkable. He takes no medications. There is no jaundice or other signs of chronic liver disease. Abdominal examination reveals no tenderness, guarding, or rebound (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause of his gastrointestinal bleeding? Labs: Blood pressure 105/65 mmHg Heart rate 110/min Temperature 36.8 °C Hb 95 130-170 g/L (Male) Platelets count 250 WBC 12 Prothrombin time 11 10-13 sec ALT 30 ALP 26 Blood urea nitrogen 14 2.8 to 8.9 mmol/L Creatinine 88 44-115 mol/L
highlight_terms_source: no jaundice or other signs of chronic liver disease
why_right: Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding, and nothing here points elsewhere: no previous episodes, an unremarkable history with no medications, no signs of chronic liver disease, normal ALT, PT and platelets, and no preceding vomiting. The raised urea with normal creatinine reflects digested blood from an upper GI source, and tachycardia with Hb 95 shows a significant bleed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Erosive gastritis is the typical source in a heavy drinker or NSAID user; his history is unremarkable and he takes no medications, so there is no trigger for it.
C. Varices need portal hypertension: stigmata of chronic liver disease, abnormal LFTs, low platelets or prolonged PT; all are normal here.
D. Mallory-Weiss tear presents with hematemesis that follows repeated or forceful vomiting; no vomiting precedes the bleeding here.
key_concept:
Upper GI bleed: pick the cause from the background clue.
  • No risk clue: peptic ulcer disease (most common)
  • Alcohol or NSAIDs: erosive gastritis
  • Stigmata of liver disease, low platelets, high INR: varices
  • Vomiting first, then blood: Mallory-Weiss tear
  • High urea with normal creatinine: upper GI bleed
exam_pearl: Sequence matters: retching before the blood means Mallory-Weiss; blood with no preceding vomiting and normal liver means PUD.

stem: Elderly man DM HTN was admitted to the ward due to acute abdomen, during laparotomy surgical team found necrotic bowel and wanted to exclude cardiac causes, his ECG showed sinus rhythm, Echo was normal. What should you do next?
why_right: Necrotic bowel in an elderly diabetic hypertensive raises acute mesenteric ischemia, and the commonest cardiac source is embolism from atrial fibrillation. A single ECG in sinus rhythm and a normal echo (no thrombus, no valve disease) do not exclude paroxysmal AF. Ambulatory Holter monitoring (24 to 48 hours or longer) is the next step to capture intermittent AF that could embolise.
why_wrong_block:
A. Exercise ECG looks for inducible ischemia in suspected stable angina; coronary disease does not cause mesenteric emboli, so it does not answer the cardiac embolic question.
C. The echo is already normal; repeating it adds nothing. If a hidden source were still suspected, transoesophageal echo (not a repeat transthoracic study) would be the step after rhythm monitoring.
D. This option was not recalled in the source, so it cannot be assessed; the decision point is excluding paroxysmal AF.
key_concept:
Embolic event (mesenteric ischemia or stroke) + normal ECG and echo: look for paroxysmal AF.
  • Holter (24 to 48 h): intermittent AF or frequent paroxysmal arrhythmia
  • Infrequent episodes: event recorder or implantable loop recorder
  • Echo (TTE then TEE): thrombus, valve disease, PFO
  • Exercise ECG: stable angina workup, not embolic source
exam_pearl: Sinus rhythm on one ECG never excludes AF; the next step is prolonged rhythm monitoring.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0107).
Compiler note: Holter monitoring (24-48 hr or longer) detects intermittent AF that can embolize = mesenteric ischemia or stroke.

stem: A 43 year old man presented to the ER complaining of lower limb weakness, urinary incontinence and difficulty walking for 3 days. T10 sensory level on neurological exam. No history of previous infection mentioned. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
why_right: Bilateral lower limb weakness, urinary incontinence and a T10 sensory level localise to the spinal cord (myelopathy), so this is a cord emergency such as compression or transverse myelitis. MRI of the spinal cord is the test of choice: it shows the cord itself, inflammation, abscess, tumour and disc, and directs urgent treatment. With no preceding infection, both compressive causes and inflammatory myelitis must be distinguished, which only MRI can do.
why_wrong_block: B. CT shows bone well but poorly shows the cord and soft tissue, so it misses myelitis and many compressive lesions; it is used only when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable (CT myelography).
key_concept:
Sensory level + paraparesis + sphincter dysfunction = spinal cord lesion: urgent MRI of the spine.
  • Compression (tumour, disc, abscess, hematoma): MRI, then steroids or decompression
  • Transverse myelitis: MRI then LP for CSF
  • MRI before LP to exclude a mass
  • CT/CT myelography only if MRI contraindicated
exam_pearl: A sensory level means cord, not brain or peripheral nerve; image the spine with MRI, not the head.

stem: Patient present with lower limb weakness, back pain and urine incontinence T10 sensory level. What is the most appropriate test to diagnose?
why_right: Back pain with lower limb weakness, urinary incontinence and a T10 sensory level is spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. MRI of the whole spine is the diagnostic test of choice because it shows the cord, the level and the cause (metastasis, abscess, disc, hematoma) and guides urgent decompression or radiotherapy.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT spine shows bony lesions but not the cord or epidural soft tissue well; it is a fallback only when MRI cannot be done.
C. Urine culture is the first step for incontinence from a suspected UTI, but here incontinence is part of a cord syndrome with a sensory level; a UTI cannot explain leg weakness and a T10 level.
key_concept:
Back pain + red flag neurology (weakness, sphincter loss, sensory level) = emergency MRI whole spine.
  • Known cancer + back pain: steroids and MRI
  • Fever + back pain: think epidural abscess or brucella/TB spondylitis, still MRI
  • Isolated incontinence without neurology: urinalysis and culture first
exam_pearl: Incontinence alone points to urine tests; incontinence with a sensory level points to the spinal cord.

stem: A 64-year-old man known to have liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C completed treatment for HCV and now has undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment. He is asymptomatic. Clinically, he has a few spider angiomata and mild splenomegaly (see lab results). Hidden labs: Platelet ~130 (less than 150); Albumin ~30 (below reference 35); ALT & AST both ~60-70; Ultrasound: mild splenomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up option?
why_right: HCV is cured (undetectable RNA 12 weeks post-treatment), but the cirrhosis persists: spider angiomata, splenomegaly, low platelets and low albumin. Cirrhosis carries an ongoing risk of hepatocellular carcinoma even after viral cure, so lifelong surveillance with liver ultrasound every 6 months (AFP is an optional adjunct) is required.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI is not the standard surveillance tool and yearly is too long an interval; MRI or triphasic CT is used to characterise a nodule found on ultrasound.
B. Viral cure does not reverse established cirrhosis; HCC and variceal risk remain, so reassurance alone is unsafe.
D. AFP alone is insensitive and the interval is wrong; it may accompany ultrasound every 6 months but never replaces it.
key_concept:
Cirrhosis of any cause = HCC surveillance with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months, even after HCV cure.
  • Nodule >1 cm on US: triphasic CT or contrast MRI
  • Typical imaging pattern: diagnose HCC without biopsy
  • Non-diagnostic imaging: other contrast study or biopsy
  • Also screen for varices with endoscopy
exam_pearl: SVR cures the virus, not the cirrhosis; surveillance continues.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is evaluated for right hip pain that started 3 weeks ago and occurs at night and with walking. Her current medications are azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine, prednisolone, and lisinopril for the last 5 years. Her examination was normal except for pain on internal rotation of the right hip. Laboratory tests including pelvic and left hip radiographs were normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of hip pain?
highlight_terms_source: pain on internal rotation of the right hip
why_right: A young woman with SLE on prednisolone for 5 years has a 3-week history of hip pain at night and with walking and pain on internal rotation, yet radiographs are normal. Chronic steroids and SLE are major risk factors for avascular necrosis, and early AVN is invisible on X-ray. MRI is the test that shows it early.
why_wrong_block:
A. Active lupus arthritis: typically a symmetric, non-erosive small-joint polyarthritis (hands, wrists), not a single hip with rotation pain and otherwise normal exam.
B. Septic arthritis affecting right hip: acute, hot, exquisitely painful joint with fever and inability to move it; a 3-week course with a normal exam apart from rotation pain does not fit.
D. Degenerative changes affecting right hip: unlikely at 30 and would usually show on X-ray; right in an older patient with mechanical pain and osteophytes.
key_concept:
Steroids + hip/groin pain + normal X-ray = avascular necrosis until MRI says otherwise.
  • Risk factors: long-term steroids, SLE, alcohol, sickle cell disease
  • Pain on internal rotation and weight bearing
  • Early X-ray normal; MRI is the most sensitive test
  • Late X-ray: crescent sign, femoral head collapse
exam_pearl: A normal hip X-ray in a steroid user does not exclude AVN; the next test is MRI.

stem: A 67-year-old man a known case of HCV cirrhosis admitted to Emergency Room with massive hematemesis. Variceal bleeding is suspected. On examination, he is drowsy with tense ascites (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 86/min, Oxygen saturation 95%. Hb 8 (130-170 g/L male), INR 1.3 (0.8-1.2). Which of the following management option has a great benefit in reducing this patient mortality?
why_right: In a cirrhotic with GI bleeding, bacterial infection (including SBP, a real risk with tense ascites) is common and drives rebleeding and death. Short-course IV ceftriaxone prophylaxis lowers infections, rebleeding and mortality, which is why the lead-in "greatest benefit in reducing mortality" points to it. Drowsiness suggests encephalopathy, often precipitated by infection and bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. Octreotide (vasoactive therapy) is given early to control variceal bleeding before endoscopy, but the classic mortality benefit asked for here is attributed to antibiotic prophylaxis.
C. He is normotensive with Hb 8; a restrictive strategy (transfuse below about 7) is used in variceal bleeding because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.
D. PPI infusion targets peptic ulcer bleeding; it does not treat variceal bleeding or lower mortality here.
key_concept:
Suspected variceal bleed: resuscitate, then vasoactive drug + antibiotics, then endoscopy.
  • Two large-bore IVs, cautious fluids, restrictive transfusion
  • Octreotide (or terlipressin) before endoscopy
  • IV ceftriaxone prophylaxis: reduces infection and mortality
  • Endoscopic band ligation
  • Unstable despite this: balloon tamponade as a bridge, then TIPS
  • Secondary prophylaxis: nonselective beta-blocker + banding
exam_pearl: "Controls bleeding" = octreotide; "reduces mortality" = antibiotics in a cirrhotic bleed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Highlighted option annotated 'MG'.

stem: A 36-year-old man presented to the clinic for evaluation of elevated liver enzyme. He is asymptomatic with no significant past medical history. He is a smoker and drinks alcohol every weekend. Examination was unremarkable (see lab results and reports). Total bilirubin 12 (3.5-16.5); AST 147 (12-40 IU/L); ALT 76 (5-40 IU/L); ALP 119 (39-117); Albumin 33 (34-56 g/L); Iron 35 (11.7-31.8 male); TIBC 34 (11.6-31.3); Ferritin 423 (20-300 male). Hepatitis screen: negative HCV, HBsAg negative with positive anti-HBs. US abdomen: enlarged liver with no focal lesion. Which of the following is the most likely cause for his underlying liver disease?
why_right: The key is the AST:ALT ratio about 2:1 (147 vs 76) in a man who drinks alcohol every weekend, with an enlarged liver and no focal lesion. This pattern is typical of alcohol-related liver injury. The mildly raised ferritin is a nonspecific finding that is common with alcohol, and the hepatitis screen is negative.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemochromatosis is tested with transferrin saturation and HFE genotype; a mild ferritin rise without diabetes, skin pigmentation or hypogonadism is more often due to alcohol, which also gives an AST-predominant pattern.
C. HCC needs a focal lesion, usually on a cirrhotic liver; ultrasound shows no focal lesion.
D. HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs positive, which means immunity (vaccination or past cleared infection), not chronic hepatitis B.
key_concept:
Transaminase pattern points to the cause.
  • AST:ALT about 2:1 + alcohol: alcohol-related liver disease
  • ALT > AST: viral hepatitis, fatty liver (NAFLD)
  • Very high AST/ALT with arthralgia, young woman: autoimmune hepatitis
  • High ferritin + high transferrin saturation: screen for hemochromatosis
  • HBsAg negative + anti-HBs positive: immune
exam_pearl: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; a mild rise in a drinker does not mean iron overload unless transferrin saturation is high.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus comes for routine follow-up visit. She was asymptomatic and currently on no medications. Her condition is stable for several years (see lab results). Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg. 24 hr urine / Protein 500 (0-150 mg/24 hr); RBC 5000 (up to 4,000 in 1 ml); Urea 20 (2.75-7.4 mmol/L); Creatinine 160 (44-115). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Repeat urine analysis in next visit
why_right: In a known SLE patient, new proteinuria 500 mg/24 h, hematuria, raised creatinine 160 and BP 140/90 indicate lupus nephritis even when she feels well. Renal biopsy is the next step because it confirms nephritis and gives the ISN/RPS class, which decides treatment (from BP control only to steroids with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide).
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-dsDNA tracks lupus activity but cannot confirm or classify renal involvement, so it does not change the next step.
C. Doppler ultrasound assesses renovascular disease or obstruction; the active urine sediment with proteinuria points to a glomerular problem, which needs tissue.
D. Watchful waiting delays treatment of possible proliferative nephritis, and rising creatinine risks irreversible kidney damage.
key_concept:
SLE + proteinuria ≥500 mg/24 h, active sediment or rising creatinine = renal biopsy.
  • Class I: BP control
  • Class II: supportive care, ACE inhibitor for proteinuria
  • Class III/IV: steroids + mycophenolate (or cyclophosphamide)
  • Class V with nephrotic proteinuria: immunosuppression
  • Hydroxychloroquine for all SLE patients
exam_pearl: Asymptomatic does not mean inactive kidneys; abnormal urine plus rising creatinine in SLE goes straight to biopsy.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with liver cirrhosis presents to the emergency with hematemesis (see report). Upper GI endoscopy: Bleeding esophageal varices. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous pharmacological treatment?
why_right: A cirrhotic patient with hematemesis and endoscopy confirming bleeding esophageal varices needs a vasoactive drug that lowers portal pressure. The lead-in asks for the "intravenous pharmacological treatment", which is octreotide (a somatostatin analogue causing splanchnic vasoconstriction), given alongside endoscopic band ligation and antibiotic prophylaxis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Propranolol (a non selective beta blocker) is oral long term secondary prophylaxis after the bleed is controlled; it is not an acute IV treatment and can worsen hypotension during active bleeding.
C. H2 blockers suppress acid and play a role in peptic ulcer disease; they do not lower portal pressure or stop variceal bleeding.
D. PPIs are the drug for bleeding peptic ulcer, the most common cause of upper GI bleeding, but they do not control variceal bleeding.
key_concept:
Acute variceal bleed sequence:
  • ABC, IV access, cautious resuscitation and transfusion
  • IV vasoactive drug: octreotide (or terlipressin), started before endoscopy
  • IV antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone): reduces mortality
  • Endoscopic band ligation
  • Uncontrolled: balloon tamponade as a bridge, then TIPS
  • Long term: non selective beta blocker (propranolol or nadolol) + repeat banding
exam_pearl: Acute bleed = IV octreotide; prevention of rebleeding = oral beta blocker. Mortality reducing drug question = antibiotic.

stem: A 63-year-old man was evaluated in the Emergency Room for 1 week of progressive shortness of breath and found to have right pleural effusion on chest X-ray. Aspiration yielded a clear transudative fluid. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: The fluid is "clear" and "transudative". Transudates come from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressure, and heart failure is by far the most common cause. Among the options, heart failure is the only transudative cause; the others cause exudates through pleural inflammation or malignant involvement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pancreatitis causes an exudative effusion, usually left-sided, with high pleural amylase.
B. Pneumonia causes an exudative (parapneumonic) effusion, typically with fever and consolidation.
D. Malignancy causes an exudative, often bloody effusion, suspected with weight loss or a known tumour.
key_concept:
First classify the fluid (Light criteria), then match the cause.
  • Exudate if pleural/serum protein >0.5 or pleural/serum LDH >0.6 (or pleural LDH >2/3 upper normal serum)
  • Transudates: heart failure (most common), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
  • Exudates: pneumonia/empyema, TB, malignancy, pancreatitis, PE
  • Transudate treatment: treat the cause (diuretics, fluid restriction)
exam_pearl: Clear transudate in an exam stem = heart failure; every infective, inflammatory or malignant cause is exudative.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with fever and shortness of breath for 2 days. She is a known rheumatoid arthritis patient on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily. Examination reveals crepitations at the right lower lung. Renal and liver function are normal. She was treated with cefuroxime with resultant significant improvement. However, her renal function is deteriorating (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause of kidney function deterioration?
why_right: Her kidney function was normal on admission and declined only after starting cefuroxime, a beta lactam, while the pneumonia improved. New AKI after a culprit drug is acute interstitial nephritis (drug hypersensitivity), classically with fever, rash and eosinophilia/eosinophiluria.
why_wrong_block:
A. Renal vasculitis presents with systemic vasculitic features (purpura, rash, pulmonary hemorrhage) and active sediment, not AKI timed to a new antibiotic.
C. Pre-renal AKI needs dehydration or hypoperfusion; she is improving clinically with no volume loss described.
D. Immune complex GN presents with hematuria, RBC casts, edema and hypertension, with no link to new drug exposure.
key_concept:
AIN = drug (or infection) induced hypersensitivity of the interstitium.
  • Culprits: beta lactams, NSAIDs, PPIs, sulfonamides, rifampicin
  • Triad: fever, rash, eosinophilia (eosinophiluria)
  • Urine: WBCs, WBC casts
  • Management: stop the drug; steroids if not improving
exam_pearl: Normal renal function at baseline then decline after a new antibiotic = AIN, even when the infection itself is improving.

stem: A 60-year-old man known to have systemic hypertension, gout, and dyslipidemia presented to the Emergency Room 5 days ago with signs of heart failure and was diagnosed with congestive heart failure and new-onset diabetes mellitus. He was stabilized and discharged on Lasix, aspirin, Plavix, and metformin. Yesterday, he came to the ER with severe pain and redness in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Examination confirms tenderness and swelling of that joint. Which of the following medications has most likely caused this new complaint?
why_right: Acute pain, redness, tenderness and swelling of the first MTP joint in a man with known gout is a gout flare. It came days after he was started on Lasix (furosemide): loop diuretics cause hyperuricemia by volume contraction and by competing with urate for tubular secretion, which precipitates flares.
why_wrong_block:
B. Clopidogrel (Plavix) does not raise uric acid and is not a recognized gout trigger.
C. Low-dose aspirin can modestly raise urate, but a newly started loop diuretic is the classic and stronger trigger; aspirin is chosen only if it is the sole urate-raising drug offered.
D. Metformin does not cause hyperuricemia or gout (its classic serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis).
key_concept:
Drug triggers of gout: anything that reduces renal urate excretion or raises urate turnover.
  • Loop and thiazide diuretics (most tested)
  • Low-dose aspirin
  • Cyclosporine, tacrolimus
  • Pyrazinamide, ethambutol
  • Starting or stopping urate-lowering therapy abruptly can trigger flares
exam_pearl: Recently started diuretic + podagra = drug-induced gout flare; furosemide beats aspirin when both are listed.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presented to the clinic with a 3-month history of lower-extremity swelling and shortness of breath. She has not had chest pain, palpitations, or fevers. On physical examination, she has jugular venous distention and engorgement with inspiration. Heart sounds are distant; a prominent early diastolic sound without gallops or murmurs is heard. Breath sounds are normal. Abdominal examination reveals shifting dullness. Pitting edema to the level of the knees is noted (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 95/min, Respiratory rate 25/min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 90%. Hb 90; Platelets 450; WBC 3; Creatinine 150; Albumin 28; C3 0.5; C4 0.1; AST 100; ALT 94. Which of the following SLE association most likely explains the current condition?
highlight_terms_source: jugular venous distention and engorgement with inspiration
why_right: The picture is right-sided heart failure (leg edema, ascites, raised JVP) with clear lungs, so look for a pericardial cause. JVP engorging "with inspiration" is Kussmaul sign and a "prominent early diastolic sound without gallops or murmurs" is a pericardial knock: both are hallmarks of constrictive pericarditis. Pericarditis is a recognised cardiac manifestation of SLE, and chronic pericardial inflammation can scar into constriction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myocardial infarction: SLE does accelerate atherosclerosis, but MI presents with chest pain, and causes left-sided failure with crackles or an S3 gallop; she has no chest pain, clear lungs and no gallop.
C. Liver failure: can cause ascites and edema, but it does not raise the JVP or produce Kussmaul sign or a pericardial knock; the mildly raised transaminases fit hepatic congestion from the heart.
D. Renal failure: lupus nephritis (creatinine 150, low C3/C4) causes edema with a low albumin, but it does not explain inspiratory JVP rise or a pericardial knock. It would be the answer if the question asked about the cause of nephrotic edema or hypocomplementemia.
key_concept:
Right heart failure signs + clear lungs + Kussmaul sign + pericardial knock = constrictive pericarditis.
  • Constriction: Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock (early diastolic), prominent x and y descents
  • Tamponade: Beck triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus, usually acute
  • Causes of pericarditis: viral, TB, uremia, post-MI, SLE and other connective tissue disease
  • SLE heart: pericarditis (most common), Libman-Sacks endocarditis, myocarditis, premature atherosclerosis
exam_pearl: An early diastolic sound with no murmur is a knock, not a valve lesion; with JVP rising on inspiration think constriction, not tamponade.

stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the Emergency Room after falling while running a marathon. He has dark urine that is dipstick positive for large blood, but no RBCs on microscopic analysis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: dipstick positive for large blood, but no RBCs
why_right: The urine dipstick heme reagent reacts with myoglobin and hemoglobin as well as red cells, so "positive for large blood" with "no RBCs on microscopic analysis" means pigmenturia, not hematuria. After the intense exertion of a marathon plus a fall, the pigment is myoglobin from muscle breakdown, so the diagnosis is exertional rhabdomyolysis. A markedly raised CK confirms it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemorrhagic cystitis: bladder bleeding gives true hematuria with RBCs on microscopy; it follows cyclophosphamide, radiation or viral infection, not exercise.
B. Glomerulonephritis: gives dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts on microscopy, often with proteinuria, edema or hypertension; microscopy here shows no RBCs.
D. Pyelonephritis: fever, flank pain, pyuria and WBC casts; any blood would show RBCs on microscopy, and there are no infective features.
key_concept:
Dipstick blood positive + no RBCs on microscopy = pigment (myoglobin or hemoglobin).
  • Exertion, crush, trauma, seizures, statins: myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis
  • Confirm with markedly raised CK
  • RBCs present: true hematuria (stone, tumor, cystitis, GN)
  • RBC casts/dysmorphic RBCs: glomerular source
  • WBC casts: pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis
exam_pearl: The discordance (dipstick positive, microscopy negative) is the whole question; any option that causes real hematuria is wrong.

stem: A 17-year-old student presented with recurrent attacks of mild wheeze and shortness of breath despite using inhaled salbutamol regularly. Which of the following is the best next step in the management?
why_right: "Recurrent attacks" of mild wheeze "despite using inhaled salbutamol regularly" means asthma uncontrolled on SABA alone (step 1). The next step is controller therapy with a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (step 2), which treats the underlying airway inflammation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral prednisolone is for acute exacerbations (short course) or the top step of chronic therapy; it is not the next step after SABA.
C. Aminophylline (theophylline) is a weak add-on with a narrow therapeutic window and is not a step 2 option.
D. Ipratropium is used in acute severe exacerbations alongside salbutamol, not as maintenance for chronic asthma.
key_concept:
Asthma stepwise care: step up when uncontrolled.
  • Classic ladder: step 1 SABA as needed, step 2 add low-dose ICS
  • Step 3: low-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 4: medium-dose ICS + LABA (or add leukotriene receptor antagonist)
  • Step 5: add-on LAMA, specialist biologics, oral steroid last
  • Current GINA: no SABA-only treatment; as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol from step 1
exam_pearl: Needing SABA "regularly" is itself the sign of poor control: add ICS, do not add more reliever.

stem: A 60-year-old man admitted to the Emergency Room with 1-day history of hematemesis. He has multiple spider angiomata on his chest with bilateral gynecomastia. Abdominal examination showed splenomegaly (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management after the initial fluid resuscitation? Blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, Heart rate 100/min, Respiratory rate 18/min, Temperature 36.6 C, Oxygen saturation 95%. Hb 8.5 (130-170 g/L male); HCT 0.23 (0.42-0.52 male).
why_right: Spider angiomata, gynecomastia and splenomegaly are stigmata of chronic liver disease with portal hypertension, so hematemesis here is variceal bleeding until proven otherwise. The lead-in says "after the initial fluid resuscitation", so the next step is upper GI endoscopy, which both confirms the source and treats it (band ligation), ideally within 12 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood transfusion: Hb 8.5 g/dL is above the restrictive threshold of 7 used in GI bleeding (over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding). It would be right with Hb below 7 or ongoing massive bleeding with shock.
C. Selective angiography: reserved for bleeding that cannot be localised or controlled at endoscopy, or for lower GI bleeding; it is not the next step for a suspected variceal bleed.
D. Nasogastric tube insertion: not routinely needed and adds nothing diagnostic or therapeutic once endoscopy is planned; it does not stop the bleeding.
key_concept:
Variceal bleed sequence: ABC and resuscitate, then medical therapy, then endoscopy.
  • Step 1: two large-bore IV lines, fluids; restrictive transfusion (target Hb about 7 to 8)
  • Step 2: vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) + prophylactic antibiotics
  • Step 3: upper GI endoscopy with band ligation
  • Failure: balloon tamponade as a bridge, then TIPS
  • Prevention after the bleed: non-selective beta blocker + repeat banding
exam_pearl: If the stem asks the FIRST step in an unstable bleeder, it is IV fluids; "after resuscitation" moves the answer to endoscopy.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presented to the clinic for follow-up of a 7-month history of chronic, nonproductive cough. She was recently diagnosed with cough-variant asthma after a methacholine challenge test. She was started on inhaled fluticasone and as-needed albuterol 2 months ago. Her cough initially improved; however, her symptoms have not fully resolved and are worsened at times, most notably when she lies down. She also noted that mild hoarseness occasionally accompanies her cough, especially when she wakes up in the morning. Examination revealed a dry cough with frequent throat clearing. The chest was clear with no wheezing. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: worsened at times, most notably when she lies down
especially when she wakes up in the morning
why_right: Her cough-variant asthma improved on fluticasone, but the residual cough is "worse when she lies down", with morning hoarseness and "frequent throat clearing" and a clear chest without wheeze. These point to gastroesophageal (laryngopharyngeal) reflux as a coexisting cause of chronic cough rather than uncontrolled asthma. Adding a proton pump inhibitor treats the remaining cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. A LABA would be right if asthma were still uncontrolled (wheeze, reduced lung function); here the chest is clear and the new features are reflux-related.
C. A nocturnal antitussive only suppresses the symptom and leaves the reflux untreated; it is not a management for an identifiable cause.
D. Repeating methacholine would only help if the asthma diagnosis were in doubt; it is already confirmed and responding to ICS.
key_concept:
Chronic cough has three big causes, often overlapping: asthma, upper airway cough syndrome, and GERD.
  • GERD clues: cough worse lying down or after meals, hoarseness, throat clearing, sour taste
  • Upper airway cough syndrome: postnasal drip, nasal congestion
  • Asthma: wheeze, nocturnal or exercise cough, reversible obstruction
  • Partial response to asthma treatment: look for a second cause before escalating
exam_pearl: Partly improved asthma cough plus hoarseness and supine worsening means add a PPI, not more bronchodilator.

stem: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for a 4-month history of dry cough, which began 4 months ago when she noted a paroxysmal onset of persistent coughing spells that make it difficult to carry on a conversation. She was initially diagnosed with allergic rhinitis and was started on a glucocorticoid nasal inhaler with no improvement. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable except for a history of dust allergies. Examination revealed normal vital signs, slight nasal congestion, and dry cough are noted during the examination. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and abdominal examination findings are unremarkable (see reports). Chest radiograph: Normal. Spirometry: Slightly reduced FEV1/FVC ratio of 70% which increased after bronchodilator challenge by 20%. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
why_right: This recall's key is methacholine challenge testing: chronic dry paroxysmal cough with dust allergy, nasal congestion and a normal chest X-ray suggest cough-variant asthma, and among the listed tests only a bronchoprovocation test actually diagnoses asthma. Allergy testing, IgE and CT do not establish asthma. Note that the stem's spirometry (FEV1/FVC 70% with 20% improvement after bronchodilator) already shows reversible obstruction, so the decision to do methacholine reflects the source's choice rather than standard need.
why_wrong_block:
A. Allergy skin testing identifies which allergen she is sensitized to but does not diagnose asthma; useful later for allergen avoidance or immunotherapy planning.
B. High-resolution CT is for interstitial lung disease or bronchiectasis; the chest X-ray is normal and nothing suggests parenchymal disease.
C. Serum IgE is nonspecific; a high level supports atopy but neither confirms nor excludes asthma.
key_concept:
Methacholine challenge is the test for suspected asthma when spirometry does not confirm it.
  • First test for suspected asthma: spirometry with bronchodilator
  • Reversibility ≥12% and ≥200 mL confirms asthma
  • Normal spirometry but high suspicion: methacholine challenge
  • Negative methacholine essentially rules out asthma (high negative predictive value)
  • Cough-variant asthma: chronic dry cough, often atopic, may lack wheeze
exam_pearl: Methacholine is chosen when spirometry is normal; if reversibility is already shown, asthma is confirmed.

stem: A young woman with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis is evaluated in the Emergency Department. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: Admit to start ceftriaxone and vancomycin
why_right: "Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis" in a young woman (not pregnant, no sepsis, tolerating oral intake) can be managed as an outpatient with an oral agent that reaches renal tissue. Ciprofloxacin is a standard first-line oral choice where local resistance allows.
why_wrong_block:
B. Clarithromycin: a macrolide for respiratory and atypical infections; it has no reliable activity against E. coli and other urinary gram negatives.
C. Admit and start carbapenem: admission and broad IV therapy are for complicated or severe disease (sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, obstruction) or known ESBL organisms, not uncomplicated pyelonephritis.
D. Admit for ceftriaxone and vancomycin: unnecessary admission, and vancomycin targets gram positives such as MRSA, which are not the usual uropathogens; this combination is an empirical regimen for meningitis or endocarditis.
key_concept:
Pyelonephritis: severity and host decide the setting.
  • Uncomplicated, tolerating orals: outpatient oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin)
  • Admit if: sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, obstruction, failed oral therapy
  • Inpatient: IV ceftriaxone
  • Nitrofurantoin: never for pyelonephritis (poor tissue levels)
exam_pearl: Pregnant woman with pyelonephritis = always admit for IV antibiotics; non-pregnant uncomplicated = outpatient oral.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the ER with symptomatic hyponatremia. Which of the following is the most serious consequence of rapid correction of hyponatremia?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the "most serious consequence of rapid correction" of hyponatremia. Raising serum sodium too fast causes osmotic demyelination, classically central pontine myelinolysis, which can be irreversible (dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, locked-in state). That is why correction of chronic or symptomatic hyponatremia must be limited per 24 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypokalemia is not the classic complication of correcting sodium too quickly and is easily treated.
B. Overshoot into hypernatremia can happen but is not the feared, irreversible neurological complication.
C. Volume overload can follow saline infusion but is manageable; it is not the most serious consequence asked for.
key_concept:
Speed of sodium correction determines the brain complication.
  • Hyponatremia corrected too fast: osmotic demyelination (CPM)
  • Hypernatremia corrected too fast: cerebral edema
  • Symptomatic hyponatremia: hypertonic 3% saline, with capped daily rise
  • Hypovolemic: 0.9% saline; SIADH: fluid restriction
  • Hypervolemic: furosemide + fluid restriction
exam_pearl: Low sodium raised fast = myelinolysis; high sodium lowered fast = cerebral edema. Do not swap them.

stem: A 79-year-old man is evaluated in follow-up for a 2-mm solitary pulmonary nodule that was incidentally discovered on imaging for chest pain 4 years ago. Follow-up chest CT scans were obtained at 1-, 2-, and 3-year intervals, and the pulmonary nodule has remained unchanged. He feels well and does not have any respiratory or constitutional symptoms. He has never smoked. Physical examination reveals normal vital signs and a normal cardiopulmonary examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
why_right: Two features make this nodule benign: it is tiny (2 mm, and a nodule of 4 mm or smaller needs no follow-up at all) and it has been unchanged for 3 years of CT follow-up. A solid nodule stable for 2 years or more is considered benign, and he is a never-smoker, so no further imaging is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeat chest CT in 1 year: annual surveillance fits a new small nodule in a high-risk patient, not a 2 mm nodule already stable for 3 years.
B. Repeat chest CT in 2 years: there is no benefit; stability beyond 2 years has already established that it is benign.
C. Repeat chest CT in 5 years: arbitrary and only adds radiation and cost; surveillance ends once benign stability is shown.
key_concept:
Solitary pulmonary nodule: decide by size, risk and growth.
  • ≤4 mm (low risk): no follow-up
  • >4 to 8 mm: serial CT surveillance (for example at 3 to 6 months)
  • >8 mm to 2 cm: PET/CT or biopsy
  • >2 cm or growing: surgical referral after PFTs
  • Solid nodule stable ≥2 years = benign
exam_pearl: A growing nodule in a heavy smoker goes to tissue diagnosis or surgery; a tiny stable one in a never-smoker needs nothing.

stem: A 38-year-old woman who is not known to have any medical illness is referred to the clinic because of a chest xray that showed prominent hilar structures bilaterally. She is having on-and-off cough but denies any history of shortness of breath, sputum production, chest pain, skin lesions, weight loss, fever, or contact with sick people. She is not a smoker. Examination reveals clear chest bilaterally (see lab results and reports). CT chest: Confirmed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, otherwise lung parenchyma was clear. CT-guided biopsy: Showed noncaseating granuloma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with non-caseating granulomas on biopsy in a young non-smoking woman is sarcoidosis. The disease is mild: only an on-and-off cough, a clear chest, and clear lung parenchyma on CT (stage I). Stage I sarcoidosis often remits on its own, so the most appropriate step is observation with follow-up.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prednisone: reserved for significant symptoms, progressive parenchymal disease, falling lung function, or serious extrapulmonary disease (cardiac, neurologic, ocular, hypercalcemia); none is present here.
C. Azithromycin: treats bacterial or atypical infection; there is no fever, sputum or infiltrate, and antibiotics have no role in sarcoidosis.
D. Anti-tuberculosis therapy: TB gives caseating granulomas with fever, weight loss or contact history; her granulomas are non-caseating and she has none of these features.
key_concept:
Sarcoidosis: treat by disease severity, not by the diagnosis alone.
  • BHL + non-caseating granuloma = sarcoidosis; caseating = TB
  • Asymptomatic or mild (stage I, clear parenchyma, normal exam): observe
  • Progressive dyspnea, interstitial infiltrates, falling PFTs: systemic glucocorticoids
  • Organ threatening disease (heart, CNS, eye, hypercalcemia): steroids
exam_pearl: Same BHL but with progressive dyspnea, crepitations and interstitial infiltrates flips the answer to glucocorticoids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Case of sarcoidosis, Stage I. When to start steroids (prednisone): dyspnea (important), progressive lung involvement, hypercalcemia, ocular involvement, cardiac/neurologic involvement.

stem: A 73-year-old with altered level of consciousness, DM, HTN, IHD, liver cirrhosis. Exam: lower limb edema, ascites. Labs: Na 125, glucose 8 mmol. Next step?
why_right: This is hypervolemic hyponatremia: Na 125 with clear volume overload (lower limb edema, ascites) in a patient with cirrhosis and IHD. Total body water and sodium are both high, so the aim is to remove water, not to give sodium-containing fluid; among these options only the loop diuretic furosemide does that (alongside fluid restriction and treatment of the cirrhosis). Glucose 8 mmol/L is near normal, so this is not pseudohyponatremia from hyperglycemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. NS: right for hypovolemic hyponatremia (vomiting, diarrhea, dry mucosa); here it would worsen ascites, edema and the cardiac load.
B. ½ NS: a hypotonic fluid that would lower sodium further and add volume; it is used for hypernatremia with dehydration, not this.
C. D5 NS: the dextrose is simply metabolised, so it acts as normal saline and adds sodium and volume to an already overloaded patient; it fits a patient needing isotonic fluid plus glucose (e.g. fasting maintenance or DKA once glucose falls), not hypervolemic hyponatremia.
key_concept:
Hyponatremia: assess volume status first.
  • Hypovolemic: normal saline
  • Euvolemic (SIADH): fluid restriction
  • Hypervolemic (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic): fluid and salt restriction + loop diuretic
  • Ascites in cirrhosis: spironolactone is the diuretic of choice, furosemide added on
  • Severe symptoms (seizures, coma): hypertonic 3% saline, slow correction to avoid osmotic demyelination
exam_pearl: Edema or ascites with low sodium means water excess: never answer saline.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Management of hypervolemic hyponatremia: fluid restriction; loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide); treat underlying cirrhosis; consider spironolactone (first-line for ascites).

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a history of asthma and allergic rhinitis has been discharged from the hospital 2 weeks ago following an acute exacerbation of bronchial asthma and reports generally poor control with a persistent nighttime cough and exertional wheeze. Her current asthma therapy is salbutamol inhaler 100 mcg prn, beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 800 mcg bd, and salmeterol 50 mcg bd. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in outpatient management?
highlight_terms_source: beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 800 mcg bd, and salmeterol 50 mcg bd
why_right: She is on PRN SABA, high-dose ICS (beclometasone 800 mcg bd) and a LABA (salmeterol), yet remains poorly controlled (night-time cough, exertional wheeze, recent admission). That is failure of step 3, so the next outpatient add-on is a leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast), which also suits her coexisting allergic rhinitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ipratropium is a short-acting antimuscarinic used in acute attacks and COPD; it is not a maintenance add-on controller in asthma.
B. Low-dose oral prednisolone is the final step, reserved for patients still uncontrolled after the add-on controller step has been tried.
D. Modified-release theophylline is an alternative add-on but is less preferred because of its narrow therapeutic index and drug interactions; LTRA is tried first.
key_concept:
Adult asthma stepwise control:
  • Step 1: SABA PRN
  • Step 2: add regular ICS
  • Step 3: add LABA (or increase ICS)
  • Step 4: add LTRA (montelukast); theophylline is an alternative
  • Step 5: oral steroid, specialist care
  • Controlled for 3 months: step down
exam_pearl: Check adherence and inhaler technique first in real life, but on the exam "uncontrolled on ICS + LABA" means add an LTRA.

stem: A 55-year-old man is evaluated for an 18-month history of intermittent, non productive chronic cough, and dyspnea with exertion. No history of fever, chest pain, heartburn, loss of appetite, or weight loss. He has smoked 1 pack daily for the last 30 years. His medical history is otherwise unremarkable, and he takes no medications. Examination revealed he is comfortable, no jugular venous distention, normal heart sounds, no murmur, clear lungs, and no lower limb edema. A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
highlight_terms_source: 18-month history of intermittent, non productive chronic cough, and dyspnea with exertion
smoked 1 pack daily for the last 30 years
chest radiograph and electrocardiogram are normal
why_right: A 30 pack-year smoker aged 55 with an 18-month chronic cough and exertional dyspnea has suspected COPD. With a normal exam, chest X-ray and ECG and no red flags, the next and diagnostic test is spirometry, showing post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 with little reversibility.
why_wrong_block:
A. A sleep study (polysomnography) is for suspected obstructive sleep apnea: snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence, obesity; none are described.
C. Chest CT is not the first test; it is for red flags (weight loss, hemoptysis, abnormal X-ray) or suspected bronchiectasis or interstitial disease.
D. Bronchoscopy is invasive and reserved for suspected endobronchial lesions, hemoptysis or tissue sampling, not first-line for chronic cough with dyspnea.
key_concept:
Suspected COPD (smoker over 40 with chronic cough or dyspnea): confirm with spirometry.
  • Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 = obstruction
  • Minimal reversibility favors COPD over asthma
  • FEV1 % predicted grades severity and tracks progression
  • Chest X-ray excludes other causes but does not diagnose COPD
exam_pearl: A normal chest X-ray does not exclude COPD; spirometry is still the diagnostic test.

stem: A 50-year-old man known to be an alcoholic presented with progressive abdominal distention and yellow discoloration of the sclera. The patient gave a history of vague abdominal pain mainly at the epigastrium. Fluid thrill was found upon examination, suggestive of ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis was done (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause of his ascites?
why_right: In an alcoholic with jaundice and ascites, the paracentesis shows a high SAAG (≥1.1 g/dL; 1.7 in the original recall) with low ascitic protein (<2.5 g/dL; 1.9 in the original recall). High SAAG means portal hypertension, and low protein points to a hepatic (cirrhotic) rather than cardiac cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nephrotic syndrome produces low SAAG ascites from hypoalbuminemia, with heavy proteinuria and edema.
B. The epigastric pain is a lure; pancreatic ascites is low SAAG with very high ascitic amylase.
D. CHF gives high SAAG ascites but with ascitic protein ≥2.5 g/dL; low protein here favors a liver cause.
key_concept:
Ascites: SAAG first, then ascitic protein.
  • SAAG ≥1.1 + protein <2.5: cirrhosis, late Budd Chiari, massive liver metastases
  • SAAG ≥1.1 + protein ≥2.5: heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, early Budd Chiari
  • SAAG <1.1: peritoneal TB, peritoneal carcinomatosis, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome
exam_pearl: High SAAG with HIGH protein flips the answer from cirrhosis to a cardiac cause.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Lab results not shown in the recall.

stem: A 33-year-old woman, who is known to have bronchial asthma and chronic sinusitis, is complaining of worsening shortness of breath and a cough that disturbs her sleep. She denied any fever, headache, or chest pain. Her medications include salbutamol MDI prn and paracetamol. Chest examination reveals bilateral expiratory wheezes. Which of the following should be added to the management plan?
why_right: She is on salbutamol MDI prn only (step 1) and now has worsening shortness of breath with a cough that disturbs her sleep, so her asthma is uncontrolled. Night waking is a marker of poor control and means she needs a regular controller. The next step is to add an inhaled corticosteroid, budesonide MDI (step 2). Chronic sinusitis is a comorbidity that should also be treated but does not change the step-up.
why_wrong_block:
A. Montelukast is a leukotriene antagonist that is a later add-on (or an alternative when ICS cannot be used, or in aspirin-sensitive asthma); ICS remains the preferred first controller.
C. Oral prednisone is for acute exacerbations (short course) or the most severe uncontrolled asthma; this outpatient has no features of a severe attack and needs a regular controller, not systemic steroids.
D. Ipratropium (SAMA) is added to nebulized salbutamol in acute severe exacerbations, not used as home maintenance therapy for asthma.
key_concept:
Asthma step-up when uncontrolled on SABA alone → add ICS.
  • Step 1: SABA prn
  • Step 2: low-dose ICS (budesonide)
  • Step 3: ICS + LABA
  • Then: leukotriene antagonist (montelukast) add-on
  • Highest step: oral corticosteroids
  • LABA without ICS increases asthma mortality
exam_pearl: Night cough or waking in a SABA-only asthmatic = uncontrolled → add inhaled steroid, not oral steroid.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 5-day history of pain and swelling in the left knee. Her pain aggravated by walking and relieved by rest. No history of small joints involvement or significant morning stiffness. On examination, left knee is swollen but not warm or erythematous. Left knee X-ray shows osteophytes and joint space narrowing. Joint aspiration reveals 280 leukocytes/mm (see lab results). BP 140/80 mmHg, Temp 36.6 °C, BMI 35 kg/m2, Hb 125, Platelets 300, WBC 11.5, ESR 8. Which of the following is the most likely arthritis?
highlight_terms_source: pain aggravated by walking and relieved by rest
why_right: Every clue is mechanical and non-inflammatory: pain "aggravated by walking and relieved by rest", no significant morning stiffness, a knee that is swollen but not warm or erythematous, X-ray osteophytes and joint space narrowing, and synovial fluid with only 280 leukocytes (below 2000 = non-inflammatory). Add age 65, BMI 35 and normal ESR, and this is osteoarthritis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rheumatoid: symmetric small-joint polyarthritis with prolonged morning stiffness (over 1 hour), raised ESR and inflammatory fluid (2000 to 50,000); none are present.
C. Gouty: acute, very painful, hot red joint (classically the first MTP) with inflammatory fluid and negatively birefringent needle crystals; this knee is cool with bland fluid.
D. Septic: hot, red, tender joint with fever and synovial WBC usually above 50,000; temperature is normal and the fluid has 280 cells.
key_concept:
Synovial fluid WBC sorts the arthritis.
  • <2000: non-inflammatory (osteoarthritis, trauma)
  • 2000 to 50,000: inflammatory (RA, gout, pseudogout)
  • >50,000: septic until proven otherwise
  • OA: pain worse with use, better with rest, stiffness <30 min
  • OA X-ray: osteophytes, joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
exam_pearl: Mechanical pain (worse with activity, better with rest) = OA; inflammatory pain is worse after rest and better with movement.

stem: A 20-year-old woman, recently married, presents with burning micturition for one week. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?
why_right: A young, recently married (sexually active) woman with burning micturition and suprapubic tenderness, no fever or flank pain, has uncomplicated lower UTI (honeymoon cystitis). Oral nitrofurantoin is first line for uncomplicated cystitis: it concentrates in the bladder, covers E. coli well and spares broader agents.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fluoroquinolones are reserved for pyelonephritis or complicated UTI because of resistance and adverse effects; not first line for simple cystitis.
C. IV gentamicin is for systemic infection such as pyelonephritis with sepsis needing admission; unnecessary for outpatient cystitis.
D. Oral beta-lactams are a less effective alternative for cystitis (and are used in pregnancy, e.g. amoxicillin per culture); not the first choice here.
key_concept:
Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman: short oral course of a bladder-targeted agent.
  • First line: nitrofurantoin (or trimethoprim/TMP-SMX if local resistance allows, fosfomycin)
  • Fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness = pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone or IV therapy
  • Pregnancy: avoid fluoroquinolones; beta-lactam or nitrofurantoin per trimester
  • Most common organism: E. coli
exam_pearl: Nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate tissue levels, so it is wrong once there is fever or flank pain (pyelonephritis).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: Newly married woman has been on her honeymoon for 1 week and is now complaining of dysuria and frequency. How will you manage? A. Ampicillin B. Nitrofurantoin C. Ciprofloxacin D. Ceftriaxone. Answer: B (Nitrofurantoin).

stem: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated because of a 3-month history of weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, and irritability. Physical examination reveals a tremor and a non-tender goiter. She has negative thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and irritability are hyperthyroid symptoms. The exam shows a non tender goiter and the Graves antibody ("negative thyroid stimulating immunoglobulins") is absent, so the best fit among the options is toxic nodular goiter (low TSH, high T4, antibody negative).
why_wrong_block:
A. A TSH secreting pituitary adenoma is rare and gives an inappropriately normal or high TSH with high fT4 (central hyperthyroidism); a toxic nodular goiter suppresses TSH.
B. Tertiary (hypothalamic) hypothyroidism causes hypothyroid symptoms; this patient is clearly hyperthyroid.
D. Graves disease gives a diffuse goiter (often with eye signs) and positive TSH receptor antibodies; a negative TSI argues strongly against it.
key_concept:
Hyperthyroid + goiter: sort by tenderness and antibody.
  • Positive TSI/TRAb, diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy: Graves
  • Negative TSI, non tender (nodular) goiter: toxic nodular goiter
  • Tender goiter, fever, high ESR, post URTI: subacute thyroiditis
  • Normal or high TSH + high fT4: TSH secreting adenoma
exam_pearl: Negative thyroid stimulating immunoglobulins is the clue that removes Graves; the goiter being non tender removes subacute thyroiditis.

stem: 50 or 55 yrs free male, incidentally found to have A-fib, HR:110, BP:110/70. What is the best treatment for him?
key_concept:
AF anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VASc (CHF 1, HTN 1, Age ≥75 2, DM 1, Stroke/TIA 2, Vascular disease 1, Age 65 to 74 1, Female 1).
  • Men 0 (women 1): no antithrombotic
  • Men 1 (women 2): consider anticoagulation
  • Men ≥2 (women ≥3): anticoagulate (DOAC preferred, warfarin acceptable)
  • Mitral stenosis or mechanical valve: warfarin
  • Rate control (HR 110): beta blocker or diltiazem
exam_pearl: Once any risk factor such as hypertension or diabetes is added, the answer moves to an anticoagulant, never an antiplatelet.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of severe epigastric pain that is worse after eating. He describes the pain as burning in nature with mild improvement with antacid therapy. Physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Hb 120 (130-170), Platelets 450, WBC 10, Urea 8.5 (2.75-7.4 mmol/L), Creatinine 65. What is the most appropriate test to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain that is worse after eating
why_right: Burning epigastric pain worse after eating with partial antacid relief suggests a peptic (gastric) ulcer. The labs add an alarm feature: Hb 120 (low) with an isolated raised urea 8.5 and normal creatinine, which points to occult upper GI bleeding (digested blood is absorbed as protein). Alarm features call for upper endoscopy, the gold standard that sees the ulcer, allows biopsy and tests for H. pylori.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT scan of the abdomen: right for suspected perforation, pancreatitis or malignancy staging; it cannot reliably show mucosal ulcers.
C. Barium swallow: right as the initial test for dysphagia from motility disorders such as achalasia; it is less accurate than endoscopy and cannot biopsy.
D. H. pylori antibody: a test-and-treat option for dyspepsia without alarm features; serology cannot confirm an ulcer or active infection, and the anemia here mandates endoscopy.
key_concept:
Dyspepsia: alarm features decide between test-and-treat and endoscopy.
  • Alarm: new symptoms at age >60, anemia, GI bleeding, weight loss, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, mass
  • Alarm present: upper endoscopy
  • No alarm, younger patient: urea breath test or stool antigen, treat if positive
  • Gastric ulcer: pain worse with food; duodenal ulcer: pain relieved by food, worse at night
  • Raised urea with normal creatinine: think upper GI bleed
exam_pearl: An isolated high urea with normal creatinine in dyspepsia is a hidden bleed clue that turns the answer to endoscopy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler highlighted Urea 8.5 (raised urea suggests upper GI bleed). A 'Q:' restatement of the same question (without platelets/urea) also highlights B. Upper endoscopy.

stem: A 32-year-old man is evaluated for a 10-month history of fatigue and diarrhoea. He has a good appetite but has unintentionally significant weight loss over the past 10 weeks. He has not had blood in the stool, melena, or other obvious source of blood loss. His systemic examinations are unremarkable. Stool is negative for occult blood (see lab results). BP 110/70, HR 80, RR 16, Temp 36.6 °C, BMI 18 kg/m2, Hb 109, MCH 20, MCV 70, Platelets 455, WBC 8, AST 30, ALT 26, Albumin 32, Total bilirubin 10. Which of the following is the best treatment?
why_right: Chronic diarrhea with weight loss despite a good appetite means malabsorption. Microcytic anemia (MCV 70) with negative occult blood means iron deficiency without blood loss, i.e. failure to absorb iron in the duodenum, and low albumin and BMI 18 support it. In a young adult this pattern is celiac disease, treated with a lifelong gluten-free diet (after confirming with tTG-IgA and duodenal biopsy while still eating gluten).
why_wrong_block:
A. Loperamide: symptom control only; it does not treat the malabsorption, anemia or weight loss and is not the definitive therapy for celiac disease.
B. Metronidazole: right for giardiasis or C. difficile; giardiasis can mimic malabsorption but needs an exposure (travel, untreated water, daycare) and a positive stool antigen, none of which is given, whereas iron deficiency with weight loss in a young adult is the classic celiac pattern.
C. Mebendazole: right for intestinal helminths (for example hookworm, which causes iron deficiency through blood loss); occult blood is negative and there is no exposure history.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: malabsorption + iron deficiency without blood loss.
  • Clinical: chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Screen: tTG-IgA (check total IgA) while on gluten
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia)
  • Treat: lifelong strict gluten-free diet
  • If symptoms persist on diet: check adherence first
exam_pearl: Iron-deficiency anemia with a negative occult blood test in a young adult means malabsorption (celiac), not a bleed.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent attacks of dyspnea and cough when exposed to dust and perfumes. Physical examination is normal except for mild expiratory wheeze on lung auscultation (see report). (Edit in examiner: she using Salmeterol) Spirometry: Reversible bronchospasm. Which of the following is most appropriate to initiate at this stage?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent attacks of dyspnea and cough when exposed to dust and perfumes
why_right: Trigger-induced dyspnea and wheeze with reversible bronchospasm confirms asthma. The examiner's edit is decisive: she is already using salmeterol, a long-acting beta agonist. A LABA must never be used alone in asthma because it increases severe exacerbations and asthma deaths, so the drug to initiate is an inhaled corticosteroid, budesonide, which treats the underlying airway inflammation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inhaled tiotropium: a LAMA added at higher steps for asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA, and a maintenance drug in COPD; it is not started before an ICS.
B. Inhaled salbutamol: the step 1 reliever for intermittent, trigger-only asthma in a patient on no therapy; with a LABA already on board, adding another beta agonist leaves the inflammation untreated.
D. Montelukast: an alternative add-on controller (useful in allergic rhinitis or aspirin-sensitive asthma), but less effective than an ICS, which is the controller of choice.
key_concept:
Asthma: an ICS is the foundation of controller therapy; never LABA monotherapy.
  • Step 1: as-needed reliever (SABA in older keys; low-dose ICS-formoterol in current GINA)
  • Step 2: low-dose ICS
  • Step 3: low-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 4: medium-dose ICS + LABA
  • Step 5: add LAMA (tiotropium), biologics, specialist referral
exam_pearl: Without the salmeterol detail (trigger-only symptoms, no treatment), the recall answer becomes inhaled salbutamol.

stem: A female patient presents with features of Cushing's syndrome (facial hair, stria, obesity) that developed over 3–4 months. Laboratory tests show both ACTH and cortisol are elevated. What is the most likely type of Cushing's syndrome?
highlight_terms_source: both ACTH and cortisol are elevated
why_right: Both ACTH and cortisol elevated means ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, which narrows the choice to pituitary adenoma or ectopic ACTH. A pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) is the most common cause of ACTH-dependent Cushing, especially in a woman with classic, gradually developing features (hirsutism, striae, obesity), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adrenal adenoma: produces cortisol autonomously, so feedback suppresses ACTH (low ACTH); it would be right if ACTH were low with an adrenal mass.
C. Exogenous steroid use: suppresses both ACTH and endogenous cortisol (unless hydrocortisone itself is measured); it is right when there is a steroid history, including potent topical creams.
D. Ectopic ACTH secretion: also high ACTH and cortisol, but typically in older men or smokers (small cell lung cancer, carcinoid) with rapid onset, very high ACTH, marked hypokalemia, weakness and hyperpigmentation, often without the full Cushingoid habitus.
key_concept:
Cushing syndrome: confirm hypercortisolism, then check ACTH.
  • Screen: 24-hour urine free cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone test, late-night salivary cortisol
  • Low ACTH: adrenal source (adenoma, carcinoma) or exogenous steroid; image the adrenals
  • High ACTH: pituitary or ectopic; do high-dose dexamethasone test and pituitary MRI
  • High-dose dex suppresses cortisol: pituitary; no suppression: ectopic
  • Equivocal: inferior petrosal sinus sampling
exam_pearl: High ACTH with severe hypokalemia, rapid onset and weight loss in a smoker flips the answer to ectopic ACTH.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (screenshot): Cushingoid features for 4 months; high cortisol 8am=840, 4pm=500; high ACTH=15; TSH=4 normal. Options: Pituitary adenoma / Adrenal adenoma / Iatrogenic / Carcinoid syndrome. Answer: A.

stem: CT scan of the brain shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the target of blood pressure acceptable In The First 24-48 Hours?
key_concept:
ICH blood pressure: lower systolic BP early, but not too far.
  • Hemorrhagic stroke: target SBP about 140 (older teaching: below 140/90).
  • Current AHA guidance: aim for about 140 and keep SBP roughly in the 130 to 150 range; driving it below 130 is linked to harm.
  • Ischemic stroke, no thrombolysis: treat only if above 220/120.
  • Ischemic stroke before/after tPA: keep below 185/110 (then below 180/105).
  • Agents: IV labetalol or nicardipine; smooth, sustained control.
exam_pearl: Do not mix up the targets: ischemic stroke tolerates high BP (220/120 or 185/110 with tPA), while ICH needs SBP brought down to about 140, not lower than 130.
